`docs/engines/unity-il2cpp.md`:

```md
# Unity (IL2CPP)

Unity games built with IL2CPP translate their C# code to C++ ahead of time; there is no Mono runtime and no IL in the game. Grembyte reads such games through the `il2cpp_*` API that `GameAssembly.dll` (or `GameAssembly.so`) exports.

- The **catalog**, **Assemblies …** and the **trace** work as for Mono, with the same signatures (`Ns.Class:Method (int,single)`).
- Code addresses in `GameAssembly` are named as the C# method they belong to: in the trace's callers, in the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) and at hook sites. IL2CPP keeps no table from code to methods, so Grembyte builds one when it attaches; function bounds come from the module's unwind data.
- The **method monitor** logs calls with arguments, results and the object they run on (with its Unity name, or the struct for a struct's methods); the **object inspector** shows fields, static fields and properties, evaluated on the game's main thread.
- **Method hooks** work as for Mono: scripts change arguments, fields and results and use `ctx.call`, `ctx.static` and `ctx.find`.

## Shared code

Many methods share one piece of code: the linker folds identical functions, and generic code is shared. Their names end in `[shared with N]`, and the trace counts them under the first; the code explorer's [engine names](../guide/code-explorer.md#names-from-the-engine) write the same as `[+N]`. A hook on such code affects every method sharing it.

## Not yet available

- The **Call method** dialog. Running methods on the game's main thread is not built for IL2CPP yet.
- The **call graph**: it reads a method's IL code, which IL2CPP does not keep.
- The **[object browser](../guide/object-browser.md#not-yet-available)**.
- Games built on Unity's ECS run much of their logic as Burst code, which method hooks do not see. In V Rising most gameplay systems are Burst-compiled; their data lies in ECS chunks rather than objects.

## Tested games

V Rising (Unity 2022.3, metadata v31, Proton).

```

`docs/engines/unity-mono.md`:

```md
# Unity (Mono)

Unity games built with Mono ship their code as .NET assemblies (`Assembly-CSharp.dll` and others) and compile it at run time. Grembyte talks to the Mono runtime in the game – `libmono`/`mono-2.0-bdwgc.dll` – through its exported API, natively on Linux and under Wine/Proton on Windows games.

Everything in the [engine overview](index.md) is available:

- The **catalog** lists the classes and methods of the game's assemblies, also offline for games read before.
- **Assemblies …** limits the catalog and the trace to chosen assemblies.
- The **trace** finds the methods a scenario calls, with preselection filters. Mono compiles every traced method first, which takes a moment for large selections; from a configurable number of methods Grembyte asks before it starts.
- The **method monitor** logs calls with arguments and results; **method hooks** change arguments, fields or results with templates of their own.
- The **call graph** shows which methods a method calls and which call it, from the IL code.
- The **object inspector** shows the fields of C# objects, and **Call method** runs a static method on the game's main thread. An enum argument is chosen from the enum's names, e.g. `StrongholdAdventure.Type`: `Minor (1)`, `Average (2)` …; a number can be typed in, too. Nested classes read as C# writes them (`StrongholdAdventure.Type`), not as Mono does (`StrongholdAdventure/Type`).

!!! tip "Try it on HermesQuest"
    HermesQuest is a small Unity Mono role-playing game made for trying out Grembyte – the running example of the [Examples](../examples/index.md) section. [Download](../examples/index.md#download) it for Linux or Windows (also for Wine/Proton). The examples walk through scans, pointer scans, value and method hooks and scripts on it.

## Object browser

**View → Object browser …** lists the game's live objects by class and opens them in the object inspector. Unity's Mono has no heap walk, so Grembyte uses Unity's own liveness calculation: it finds the objects reachable from static fields and from Unity's objects, and the game stands still for a moment while it runs. The [object browser guide](../guide/object-browser.md#unity-mono) explains it.

## 32-bit games

32-bit Unity games under Wine/Proton work with all Mono tools: catalog, trace, method monitor, object inspector, **Call method** and the object browser. Mono features always go through the Frida gadget; value hooks and the write watch use ptrace in 32-bit games (see [backends](../guide/write-watch.md#backends-frida-or-ptrace)).

## Games that sleep out of focus

Some Unity games stop running frames when their window loses focus (Unity's *Run In Background* switched off), e.g. Might & Magic X – Legacy in window mode. Getters, **Call method**, Unity object names and the object browser run on the game's main thread, which then waits for the next window message instead of running game code. Grembyte wakes it with an empty window message and does its work there, so these tools also work while you are in Grembyte; the game itself stays paused.

## Mono and value hooks

The [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md#mono-games-static-fields-as-chain-bases) can start chains in the static fields of the classes in the marked assemblies, which Mono keeps on the heap.

Code compiled by Mono lies in no module and moves with every start. Grembyte therefore names a hit of the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) in JIT code by its C# method, and a [hook](../guide/hooks.md) with a pointer chain remembers that method: after a restart Mono compiles it and the hook is installed in it right away.

## Example: Pillars of Eternity

Pillars of Eternity (native Linux build) shows what the engine tools do in a real game.

### A cheat function from the catalog

Its assembly keeps a static class `Scripts` with the developers' console commands. Typing `scripts player` into the catalog's filter finds them, among them `GivePlayerMoney (int)`:

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Catalog in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-catalog-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Catalog in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-catalog-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The catalog filtered for <code>scripts player</code>: 8 of 22077 methods.</figcaption>
</figure>

A [script](../guide/scripts.md) with a number parameter `amount` calls it. **Copy signature** in the catalog gives the name to paste:

```js
const value = Math.trunc(ctx.args.amount);   // the method takes an int
ctx.call("Scripts:GivePlayerMoney (int)", value);
return "Gold increased by " + value;
```

`ctx.call` ignores the parameter list `(int)`; it picks the method with as many parameters as arguments given. `Math.trunc` cuts off decimals that someone may type into the number field.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script giving money in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-script-money-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Script giving money in Pillars of Eternity](../assets/photos/mono-pillars-script-money-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The script, run with its <a href="../../guide/scripts/#hotkeys">hotkey</a> <code>Ctrl+Shift+G</code>: its result in the log, and the game's own message – the money went through the game's code.</figcaption>
</figure>

### A method hook on the damage

Every hit in Pillars of Eternity goes through `Health:DoDamage(DamageInfo damage, GameObject attacker)`. The [method monitor](index.md#method-monitor) shows a call with its arguments: the object hit (`this`), the `DamageInfo` and the attacking GameObject. **Object details** opens each in the object inspector, where the field `m_damageBase` of `DamageInfo` turns up.

A method hook **before the call** changes that field before the game uses it. The attacker is a GameObject; `component("CharacterStats")` gives its component with the character's stats, whose `IsPartyMember` tells the party from its enemies:

```js
const stats = ctx.args.attacker && ctx.args.attacker.component("CharacterStats");
const base_old = ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase;

if (stats && !stats.IsPartyMember)
  ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase *= 0.3;   // enemies deal 30 %

if (stats && stats.IsPartyMember)
  ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase *= 20;    // the party deals 20 times the damage

ctx.log(`Base damage changed from ${base_old} to ${ctx.args.damage.m_damageBase}`);
```

`ctx.args.attacker && …` guards against hits without an attacker (traps, falling), where the argument is `null`.

      <figcaption>One call of <code>Health:DoDamage</code>: a companion hits a forest troll.</figcaption>
    </figure>

`docs/engines/unreal.md`:

```md
# Unreal Engine

Grembyte supports Unreal Engine 4.23 and later, 64-bit, natively and under Proton. It finds the engine's reflection data – `FNamePool` and `GUObjectArray` – in memory by its shape, without signatures, SDK dumps or a mod loader, and measures the layout of objects, properties and functions on the game itself.

- The **catalog** lists the classes and UFunctions with C++ parameter types, grouped by package: `/Script/<Module>` for C++ classes, the first folder for Blueprints (`/Game/Blueprints`).
- **Assemblies …** (here: packages) and the **trace** work as for Mono. The trace hooks the exec thunks of native UFunctions and gives every Blueprint function a hookable stub of its own. It sees calls from Blueprints and through `ProcessEvent` (events, delegates), not C++ calling C++ directly – the [native trace](../guide/native-tools.md) sees those.
- The **method monitor** logs UFunction calls with the object they run on (with its UObject name), arguments and result; the **object inspector** shows the UProperties of objects and structs. Arguments come from the parameters `ProcessEvent` passes, or, when a Blueprint calls a native function, from the bytecode of the call (variables and constants; other arguments show as `?`).
- **Method hooks** change arguments (from `ProcessEvent`'s parameters, or ref arguments from Blueprint code) and fields before a call, or the result after it. Their scripts can call UFunctions: `obj.call("Function", ...args)` runs it through `UObject::ProcessEvent` on the game thread, and `ctx.find("ClassName")` gives a live object of a class, e.g. the game's cheat manager.

## Call method

**Call method** runs a UFunction through `ProcessEvent` on the game thread: a static one on its class default object, an instance one (from the catalog or favorites) on a live object of its class – the first one found, or the one whose name or address you type in.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Call method](../assets/screenshots/method-call-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption><code>AlabamaCheatManager:GiveHealth</code> in Avowed.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Parameter type | Entered as |
| --- | --- |
| `FString`, `FName` | text |
| `bool` | checkbox |
| enums | chosen from their names, or as a number |
| structs of numbers (`FVector`, …) | `1 2 3` or `X=1; Z=3` |
| outputs | nothing; shown after the call |

Not possible as arguments: `TArray`, `TMap`, `TSet`, `FText` and delegates.

Many shipping builds keep their cheat manager: in Avowed `BP_CheatManager_C` (an `AlabamaCheatManager`) has 147 functions with code, such as `GiveHealth`, `AddCurrency` and `ToggleUnlimitedStamina`.

## Object browser

**View → Object browser …** lists every live object of the game by class, read from `GUObjectArray`, and opens them in the object inspector. Packages, a filter on class and object names, singletons and templates are explained in the [object browser guide](../guide/object-browser.md#unreal-engine).

## GAS attributes

Games built on Unreal's Gameplay Ability System keep values such as health, strength or damage multipliers as *attributes*. **View → GAS attributes …** shows the player's attribute sets with base and current value, live. The window can be [docked](../guide/tools.md#docking-windows) beside the scanner.

!!! note "Games without GAS"
    Not every Unreal game keeps its values with GAS, even when the plugin is loaded: Queen's Domain, for one, keeps health, level and potions in plain fields of the player character. The table then stays empty and the window says:

    > The player has no attribute sets: the game does not keep its values with the Gameplay Ability System. They may be fields of the player: "Inspect player" shows them.

    The line below the table names the player and its class. **Inspect player** opens the player's object in the [object inspector](index.md#object-inspector); its filter finds a field such as `Health` among hundreds, which can then be read, changed or put on the address list.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![GAS attributes](../assets/screenshots/gas-attributes-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![GAS attributes](../assets/screenshots/gas-attributes-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

GAS computes the current value anew from the base value and the active effects, so writing it into memory does not last. A base value set in the window goes through the game's own setter instead (found by its parameters; in Avowed `AlabamaAbilitySystemBlueprintLibrary:SetFloatAttributeBaseFromAbilitySystemComponent`), and the active effects keep counting: in Avowed `DamageOutgoingMult` 3 with a +40 % bonus deals 4.2 times the damage.

The search finds sets and attributes by name. **Only changed** shows only attributes whose current value differs from the base (effects act on them) or that are held; the current value is orange where effects change it. **Live** reads the values every second, **Refresh** once.

**Hold** keeps the selected attributes at their base value against the game resetting it (loading, levelling up) with a script in the [Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) tab, also the next time Grembyte attaches; the column **Held** marks them. **Release** deletes those scripts; the values stay until the game changes them. Scripts can do the same with `ctx.gas.get("Might")` and `ctx.gas.setBase("AttributeSetCore.Might", 14)`.

Some games give a set's object a new number on every load, as Gothic 1 Remake does with `AttributeSet_Health_2147445233`. Scripts may leave the number out (`ctx.gas.get("AttributeSet_Health.Health")`), and hold scripts from the window do so themselves. `ctx.gas.findSet(/^AttributeSet_Health/)` gives the set's current full name.

In Avowed, filter the window for `might` and double-click the base value: the character sheet follows at once.

      ![Might 1 in Avowed](../assets/photos/unreal-avowed-gas-before-dark.webp#only-dark)
      ![Might 1 in Avowed](../assets/photos/unreal-avowed-gas-before-light.webp#only-light)
      <figcaption>Might at its base value 1.</figcaption>
    </figure>

=== "After"

# Test game: code explorer

This example uses the [code explorer](../guide/code-explorer.md) on the small test game of the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md), `test_app/dummy_game.c`. It goes from a button's text to the function that pays out gold, and ends with a native script that gives 500 gold through that function. It takes about ten minutes and needs no knowledge of assembly beyond reading along.

!!! tip "Reading assembly"
    The [assembly quick reference](../reference/assembly.md) explains registers, operands and the instructions this page shows, and how to read a function line by line – `add_gold` and `on_treasure` included.

The test game is a native C program without an engine, like a game with an engine of its own. Grembyte has no catalog of classes for it: the way in is its machine code.

## Build and start the game

As in the tutorial (needs `gcc` and the GTK 3 development packages):

```bash
mkdir -p build
gcc -O2 test_app/dummy_game.c -o build/dummy_game.exe $(pkg-config --cflags --libs gtk+-3.0)
./build/dummy_game.exe
```

Attach Grembyte to `dummy_game.exe` and open **View → Code explorer …**. The module `dummy_game.exe` is chosen already; after a moment the status line reads something like *dummy_game.exe: ELF, 64-bit, image base 0x400000; 45 functions, 65 strings, 262 references.*

!!! note "Your addresses differ"
    The addresses and byte patterns on this page come from GCC on Fedora, which builds this command without position-independent code (image base `0x400000`). Another compiler version, other flags or a distribution that builds position-independent executables by default (Debian, Ubuntu: image base `0`) give other addresses and patterns; the steps are the same. Copy patterns from your own code explorer, not from this page.

## 1. From the button to its handler

The game has a button **Find treasure (+20-30 gold)**. Its text has to be somewhere in the program:

1. Type `treasure` into the filter of the **Strings** tab and select `Find treasure (+20-30 gold)`.
2. The references list shows one instruction, in `on_activate`: the function that builds the window. Double-click it.

The disassembly opens at the instruction loading the text, right before the call that creates the button:

```text
0x4009a1  call 0x4003e0                 gtk_button_new_with_label
0x4009a6  mov edi, 0x4019cd             "Find treasure (+20-30 gold)"
```

Further down, the same function connects every button to its handler. The comments name what the instructions load:

```text

0x400a56  mov esi, 0x401a12             "clicked"
0x400a5b  call 0x400450                 g_signal_connect_data
```

It rolls a random number, calls `add_gold` with it and refreshes the window. Double-click the `add_gold` line:

```text
0x4006d0  mov rax, qword ptr [rip + 0x2a31]    g_game
0x4006d7  mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]

0x4006dd  ret
```

Four instructions, and they are the pointer chain of the tutorial: read the global `g_game`, take the pointer at `+0x28` (the player), add the first argument (`edi`) to the value at `+0x0` (the gold). The [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md) finds the same chain from the other end.

**Callers** lists two calls of `add_gold`: from `on_treasure` and from `on_gold_add` (the **Gold +100** button). **Back** returns to the previous function.

## 4. What add_gold takes

To call a function from a script, `ctx.native.fn` needs its return type and argument types. (Registers, their 32- and 8-bit names and the instructions below are explained in the [assembly quick reference](../reference/assembly.md).) A game without debug information states them nowhere; they are read from the machine code. That works well, because the [calling convention](../reference/assembly.md#calling-conventions) fixes where arguments arrive: on Linux integers and pointers come in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`, `float` and `double` in `xmm0`–`xmm7`, and the result goes back in `rax` or `xmm0` (Windows and Wine/Proton use `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9` and `xmm0`–`xmm3`). The first argument of a C++ method is `this`.

### Which argument registers does the function read before writing them?

```text
mov rax, qword ptr [rip + 0x2a31]   ; g_game: a global, no argument
mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]
add dword ptr [rax], edi            ; edi is read without being set first: argument 1
ret
```

- `edi` is read, so there is a first argument. `rsi`, `rdx` and the others do not appear: there is no second one.
- **Width:** `edi` is the 32-bit half of `rdi`, so the argument is an `int`. All of `rdi` would mean a pointer or a 64-bit integer; a pointer gives itself away by being used as an address, as in `[rdi + 0x28]`. Only `dil` (8 bits, often in `test dil, dil`) means a `bool` or `uint8`.
- **Sign:** `add` does not tell; `movsxd` or a signed comparison (`jl`, `jg`) would. `"int"` is right either way.
- **Return value:** `rax` holds something at the `ret`, but only the player pointer as an intermediate result. Whether it is a return value only the callers tell.

### What do the callers set before the call, and read after it?

**Callers** leads to them. In `on_treasure`:

```text
call rand
…                              ; the remainder of rand() % 11
lea  edi, [rax + 0x14]         ; edi = remainder + 20: the argument, 20 to 30 gold
call add_gold
add  rsp, 8                    ; eax is not used after the call
jmp  refresh_ui
```

- Before the call only `edi` is set: one argument, and its meaning, the amount of gold.
- After the call nobody reads `eax`: the function returns nothing (`"void"`). Callers reading `eax` or `rax` right after a call (`test eax, eax`, `mov [...], eax`) show a return value; `al` alone a `bool`, `xmm0` a `float` or `double`.
- With several callers, compare them: a register all of them set is an argument; one only some set is chance.

So `add_gold` is `void add_gold(int amount)`, in a script `n.fn(at, "void", ["int"])`.

### Grembyte guesses it too

The code explorer does this reading for every function it opens: the line above the disassembly says *Guessed from the code: void add_gold(int rdi)*. The [native function monitor](../guide/native-tools.md#native-function-monitor) uses the same guess: its column **Signature (guessed)** reads `void (int rdi)`, the log shows `int rdi=23` instead of four registers, and the result `—` instead of whatever `rax` happens to hold. For `change_mana` (**Cast spell**, and every second while the mana regenerates) it reads `void (float xmm0)`, and the log shows the amount: `float xmm0=-7.5`, or `0.13`. **Copy script** writes the guess into the `n.fn` line (step 5).

It is a guess from the code in address order, so the ways above to check it still matter: a function that only passes an argument on to another one (a tail call) shows fewer arguments than it takes, and one that callers reach only through a pointer (like `on_treasure`, a GTK callback) gets its return type from its own code, marked with `?`. Untick **Guessed signature** in the monitor to see the raw registers again.

### Check it while the game runs

The [native function monitor](../guide/native-tools.md#native-function-monitor) (step 3) logs each call's argument registers, its result and its caller, and shows the bytes an argument points to if it is an address. For `add_gold` the first argument reads 20 to 30 with every **Find treasure**: the gold. That confirms a guess before a script calls the function itself.

### Hints in the game itself

- **Symbols:** Linux games are often not stripped. A C++ name such as `_ZN6Player7AddGoldEi` turns into `Player::AddGold(int)` with `c++filt`, `this` included. The test game's symbols are plain C names: they give the name, not the types.
- **Assert and log texts:** some games keep whole signatures in their messages, e.g. `int __cdecl RegisterCVar(const struct String &, …)`. The **Strings** tab finds them.
- **Imported functions** (`SDL_…`, `gtk_…`, `kernel32.dll!…`) have documented signatures, which tell what a function does with the values it passes on.

### When a guess is wrong

| Wrong guess | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| More arguments than the function takes | Harmless: it ignores them. |
| Fewer arguments | It reads whatever is in the register: a wrong number, or for a pointer most likely a crash. |
| A number where it expects a pointer, or the other way round | Almost certainly a crash once the function uses the value as an address. |
| `"void"` instead of a return type | Only the result is lost. |
| A return type for a `void` function | A random number; no harm done. |

This is why small functions with plain arguments, like `add_gold`, are the best ones to call from a script. A function that expects an object (`this`, or another pointer) is only worth calling if the script has that object, for example from a global like `g_game`.

## 5. Call it from a script

With `add_gold` open, click **Copy script**. The clipboard now holds:

```js
// add_gold: found by its bytes, not by a fixed address
const n = ctx.native;
const at = n.scan("48 8B 05 ?? ?? ?? ?? 48 8B 40 28 01 38");
// Guessed from the code, check it in the disassembly: void add_gold(int rdi)
const fn = n.fn(at, "void", ["int"]);
// fn(1);
return String(at);
```

The pattern is the function's first bytes; the address of `g_game` inside the first instruction became `?? ?? ?? ??`, because a new build of the game moves it. The `n.fn` line carries the signature Grembyte guessed: one `int` in `edi`, nothing returned, as step 4 found by hand. Do the same for `refresh_ui` (open it from `on_treasure`, **Copy pattern**), so the window shows the new gold at once.

In the **Scripts** tab create a script, **When:** *Only when run by hand*, with this code (use your own patterns):

```js
// Test game: 500 gold through the game's own functions
const n = ctx.native;
// add_gold(int amount): mov rax, [g_game] / mov rax, [rax+0x28] / add [rax], edi
const addGoldAt = n.scan("48 8B 05 ?? ?? ?? ?? 48 8B 40 28 01 38");
const addGold = n.fn(addGoldAt, "void", ["int"]);
// refresh_ui(): shows the new values in the window
const refreshUi = n.fn(n.scan("53 BA ?? ?? ?? ?? BE 00 01 00 00 48 81 EC 00 01 00 00"), "void", []);
addGold(500);
refreshUi();
// Read the gold back: g_game is what add_gold's first instruction loads
const gGame = n.rip(addGoldAt, 3, 7);
return `Gold: ${gGame.readPointer().add(0x28).readPointer().readS32()}`;
```

**Run now**. The game shows 500 more gold, and the log reads:

```text
No engine adapter: scripts run natively each time g_main_context_iteration returns on the game's main thread.
= "Gold: 600"
```

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The script in the <strong>Scripts</strong> tab, run twice: each run gives 500 gold through <code>add_gold</code>](../assets/screenshots/example-script-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![The script in the <strong>Scripts</strong> tab, run twice: each run gives 500 gold through <code>add_gold</code>](../assets/screenshots/example-script-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The script in the <strong>Scripts</strong> tab, run twice: each run gives 500 gold through <code>add_gold</code>. The first run says where native scripts run in this game.</figcaption>
</figure>

The game has no engine adapter, so Grembyte runs the script on the game's main thread when GTK's main loop returns from an event (see [scripts in native games](../guide/scripts.md#scripts-in-native-games)). `n.rip(addGoldAt, 3, 7)` reads the RIP-relative address in `mov rax, [rip + …]`: the displacement starts at byte 3 of the 7-byte instruction. For an instruction like that, **Copy script** writes this line itself.

The script keeps working after **New game**: it calls the game's code instead of writing to an address, and the game's code always finds the current player.

!!! example "Next: the way to the gold"
    [A pointer chain from the code](dummy-game-pointer-chain.md) reads the chain `g_game → 0x28 → 0x0` from `add_gold`, puts the gold on the address list so it survives **New game**, and explains how to tell a step of a chain from an offset.

## What carries over to real games

- A **text** the game shows or logs (a menu entry, a message, a console command) leads to the code using it. In a game without symbols the functions are called `sub_…`; the strings, the imports (`gtk_…`, `SDL_…`, `kernel32.dll!…`) and the callers still tell what they do.
- **Short functions that change one value**, like `add_gold`, are what scripts call best: one argument, no object to pass.
- **Patterns** survive updates that do not change the function itself. If a script reports that its pattern is no longer found, open the function again in the code explorer and copy the new one.

```

`docs/examples/dummy-game-pointer-chain.md`:

```md
# Test game: a pointer chain from the code

The gold of the [test game](../getting-started/first-hook.md) lives on the heap: its address changes with every start and every **New game**. What stays the same is the way there – a *pointer chain*. The [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md) finds it by searching the game's memory. This example finds the same chain another way: by reading the code that changes the gold. The game's own code knows the way, because it has to walk it every time.

It starts at `add_gold`, the function the [code explorer example](dummy-game-code-explorer.md) found behind the button **Find treasure**, and ends with the gold on the address list, found again after every **New game** and every restart. The second half explains, without any knowledge of assembly, how to tell a step of a chain from a plain offset – the one thing that is easy to get wrong.

Build and start the game and open **View → Code explorer …** as in the [code explorer example](dummy-game-code-explorer.md#build-and-start-the-game).

!!! note "Your addresses differ"
    The addresses on this page come from GCC on Fedora, which links the test game at a fixed address (image base `0x400000`). Another compiler or distribution gives other numbers; the steps are the same. Take the numbers from your own code explorer.

## 1. The code that changes the gold

In the **Functions** tab, type `gold` into the filter and double-click `add_gold`. Then switch from **Assembler** to **Pseudocode (guess)**:

```c
void add_gold(int32_t a1 /* rdi */)
{
    *(int32_t *)(*(uint64_t *)(g_game + 0x28)) += a1; // 0x4006db  g_game → 0x28 → 0x0
}
```

One line: "add `a1`, the amount, to the number at …". The comment after `//` holds two things:

- `0x4006db` is the address of the instruction that does it – in the code, not where the gold is.
- `g_game → 0x28 → 0x0` is the way to the gold: the pointer chain we are after. The code explorer writes it down for every line that reaches memory from a global variable.

The disassembly says the same in three instructions:

```text
0x4006d0  mov rax, qword ptr [rip + 0x2a31]    g_game
0x4006d7  mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]
0x4006db  add dword ptr [rax], edi
```

## 2. Reading the line from the inside out

A line like this is read from the innermost parentheses outwards, the order in which the processor does it:

| Piece | What happens | Step of the chain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `g_game` | Read the global variable `g_game`. It holds an address: where the `Game` object lies on the heap. | Start: `g_game` |
| `g_game + 0x28` | Go `0x28` bytes further into the `Game` object. Nothing is read yet. | the offset `0x28` |
| `*(uint64_t *)( … )` | Read the 8 bytes there. They are again an address: where the player's `Character` lies. | `→` |
| `*(int32_t *)( … )` | The 4-byte number at that address, `0x0` bytes into the `Character`: the gold. | `→ 0x0` |
| `+= a1` | Add the amount. | – |

The source of the test game confirms it (`test_app/dummy_game.c`): `Game` has a 32-byte name and a 4-byte round counter, then 4 bytes of padding and the pointer `player` at `0x28`; `Character` starts with `gold`.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![add_gold as pseudocode, the references to g_game above it](../assets/screenshots/example-chain-add-gold-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![add_gold as pseudocode, the references to g_game above it](../assets/screenshots/example-chain-add-gold-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption><code>add_gold</code> as pseudocode with its chain <code>g_game → 0x28 → 0x0</code>. Above it, after <strong>Go to</strong> <code>g_game</code>: the twelve instructions that use the global, and in the header where it lies, <code>dummy_game.exe+0x3108</code>.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 3. Where the chain starts

A chain has to start somewhere that does not move: a global variable inside the program's file. `g_game` is one. Type `g_game` into the field at the top and click **Go to**. The header of the references reads:

```text
References to 0x403108 (g_game, dummy_game.exe+0x3108): 12.
```

`dummy_game.exe+0x3108` is the start of the chain: `0x3108` bytes into the module `dummy_game.exe`. Grembyte writes chains with the module, not with `0x403108`, because a program built position-independent (most Linux distributions, all Windows games with ASLR) is loaded at a different address with every start – the offset inside the module stays.

So the chain of the gold is:

```text
dummy_game.exe+0x3108 → 0x28 → 0x0
```

!!! tip "Every user of the gold, in one list"
    The references to `g_game` lead to every function that works with the game state: `refresh_ui` shows the whole player – `g_game → 0x28 → 0x4` the hit points, `→ 0x14` the mana, `→ 0x18` the experience. Same way, different last offset.

## 4. On the address list

In the main window, below **Tracked addresses**, click **Pointer chain …** and type the chain. Arrows are typed as `->`, `=>` or `:`, whatever is easiest:

```text
dummy_game.exe+0x3108 -> 0x28 -> 0x0
```

Choose the type `int32` (the line read `int32_t`) and a description. Below the input the dialog says where the chain leads right now. **Add**.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The chain of the gold in the dialog Pointer chain …](../assets/screenshots/example-chain-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![The chain of the gold in the dialog Pointer chain …](../assets/screenshots/example-chain-dialog-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The chain read from <code>add_gold</code>, entered by hand: it leads to the player's gold on the heap.</figcaption>
</figure>

Now check it in the game: **Gold +100** changes the value on the list. **New game** puts the player somewhere else on the heap – the address column changes, the value is still the gold. After a restart of the game the entry finds it again, too. It is the same chain the [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md) finds, only read from the code instead of searched in memory.

## Chain or offset?

A chain has two kinds of numbers, and the whole difference is whether something is **read**.

### The picture

Think of the game's memory as one very long street. Every byte is a house with a number.

- An **offset** (written `+`) means: from here, walk that many houses further. Nothing is read, you only count. `0x403108 + 0x28` is simply house number `0x403130`.
- An **arrow** (written `→`) means: go into the house, read the note on the table – it holds a house number – and go *there*. Where you end up depends on what the note says right now. That is why a chain still works when the game moves the player: the game updates the note.

Read like that, `dummy_game.exe+0x3108 → 0x28 → 0x0` says: go to house `g_game` and read the note (where the game is). Walk `0x28` houses further and read the note there (where the player is). Walk `0x0` houses further: here lies the gold.

`dummy_game.exe+0x3108 + 0x28` would be something else entirely: the house `0x28` behind `g_game` – just other memory of the program, not the player.

### How the code tells you

**A step of the chain is a read whose result is then used as an address.** In the code explorer that looks like this:

| In the disassembly | In the pseudocode | In the chain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mov rax, qword ptr [rip + …]`, comment `g_game` – reads the global | `rax = g_game;` | the start, read with an arrow after it |
| `mov esi, 0x403108` or `lea rax, [rip + …]` – only the address, nothing read | `&g_game` | an address: offsets after it are added with `+` |
| `mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]` – 8 bytes read, then used inside `[ ]` | `rax = *(uint64_t *)(rax + 0x28);` | `→ 0x28` |
| `lea rbx, [rax + 0x14]`, `add rax, 0x14` – counted, not read | `rbx = rax + 0x14;`, `rax += 0x14;` | `+ 0x14`: the same object, the last offset changes |
| `add dword ptr [rax], edi` – the value itself, 4 bytes | `*(int32_t *)rax += a1;` | the end: the last offset, here `0x0` |

Three rules of thumb:

1. **Square brackets read** (in the pseudocode: a `*(…)` around something). The exception is `lea`: it only computes what is in its brackets.
2. **8 bytes read and then used as an address** (`qword`, `uint64_t`; in a 32-bit game 4 bytes, `dword`) is a pointer: an arrow. A 4-byte `int`, a `float` or a `double` that is only used as a number is the value itself: the chain ends there.
3. **Count the pointer reads.** Every read of an address – the global at the start counts too – is one arrow. `*(int32_t *)(*(uint64_t *)(g_game + 0x28))` reads `g_game` and the player pointer: two arrows, `→ 0x28 → 0x0`. The last read, of the gold itself, is no arrow; it only says where the chain ends.

The test game has both kinds in one place: `main` prints where the gold is, with `printf("g_game @ %p (pointer chain: g_game -> +%#zx player -> +%#zx gold)", &g_game, 40, 0)`. In the references to `g_game` that is `mov esi, 0x403108` – the address of `g_game`, not its content, so the `&`. `add_gold` instead reads the content: `mov rax, qword ptr [rip + 0x2a31]`.

### When a register already holds the object

Often a function does not read the global itself but gets the object handed over – as an argument `a1`, in `rcx` under Windows (`this` in C++). The code of that function alone does not tell where the object lies. The [native function monitor](../guide/native-tools.md#native-function-monitor) does: select the instruction, click **Monitor**, let the game run it, and look at the register.

- **The value lies in a module** – the column **Meaning** shows e.g. `game.exe+0x43e600`: the object itself is a global. Its field is at that address **plus** the offset, `game.exe+0x43e600+0xb0`. No arrow: nothing was read to get there.
- **The value lies on the heap** – no module in **Meaning**: someone read it from somewhere. **Callers** shows who calls the function; follow them until a line reads a global (`rax = g_game;`). Each read on the way is one arrow. If that gets long, let the [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md) do the searching.

### If you mixed them up

- **A `+` where an arrow belongs** lands in the memory right behind the global. The value on the list is some other number of the program and does not follow the game.
- **An arrow where a `+` belongs** takes a number for an address. The dialog **Pointer chain …** then says the chain leads nowhere right now, or the list shows nonsense.

Both are harmless – only reading is involved. Fix the entry and try again: the preview in the dialog shows at once whether the chain leads somewhere.

## What carries over to real games

- **Chains in real games are longer**, and every function shows only its part of the way. **Callers** leads to where the object comes from; the pointer scan is the check from the other end.
- **Stripped games have no names.** Globals show up as `*(uint64_t *)0x14043e600`, and the comment writes the chain with the module right away: `game.exe+0x43e600 → 0x28 → 0x0`.
- **32-bit games** have 4-byte pointers: a step of the chain reads a `dword`, not a `qword`.

```

`docs/examples/hermesquest-hooks.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: hooks

Grembyte has two kinds of hooks, and HermesQuest is built to show both:

| | Value hook | Method hook |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catches | one **write instruction**, found with the write watch | one **method** of the game, found in the catalog |
| Sees | the old and the new value | the method's arguments, its object (`this`) and its result |
| Works in | every game | Unity (Mono, IL2CPP) and Unreal games |
| Script | a [hook template](../guide/templates.md) | a [method script](#method-hooks) |

The examples assume you have tracked Gold, Mana and Health as in [Scans and pointer scan](hermesquest-scans.md), ideally with pointer chains.

## Value hooks

### Ten times the gold

1. Right-click "Gold" → **Address watch (writes)**.
2. Kill an enemy in the game. The watch lists one row: the instruction that added the gold. In a Mono game the code was compiled at run time and lies in no module, so Grembyte names it by its C# method: `AddGold` of the class `Character`, plus an offset into it.
3. Select the row → **Create hook …**, template **Multiplier**, factor `10`, **Increases only**.

From now on every kill brings ten times the gold. The column **Last** in the Hooks tab shows each write as *old → written by the game ⇒ stored*, e.g. `12 → 17 ⇒ 62`.

What happens: the game executes `Stats.Gold += amount`. The hook sits on exactly that instruction and replaces the result with `old + (new − old) × 10`. The game's own code and the log don't know about it – the log still says "5 gold", the character sheet shows the multiplied amount.

!!! tip "After a restart"
    Code compiled by Mono moves with every start. A value hook in such code remembers its C# method: when HermesQuest starts again, Grembyte has Mono compile `AddGold` and installs the hook in it right away. This needs the tracked address to have a pointer chain; see [Hooks after a restart](../guide/hooks.md#after-a-restart).

### Protecting the player, not the enemies

Health shows the classic problem of **shared code**: player and enemies are both `Character`, and the same instruction in `TakeDamage` lowers everyone's health.

1. Track the player's Health (`float`, 50 at the start; take a hit, then **Decreased**).
2. Right-click it → **Address watch (writes)**, then let an enemy hit you, and rest with **R**.

The watch shows more than one row, because three methods write health:

| Method | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Character:TakeDamage` | every hit, on player and enemies |
| `Character:Heal` | resting with R |
| `Character:LevelUp` | a new level refills health |

Select the `TakeDamage` row → **Create hook …**. Instead of a built-in template, use one of your own: in **View → Hook templates …** create a template "Halve damage" with this function:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```

Read it as: *if the value goes down (`ctx.delta < 0`), store the old value plus half the change, otherwise keep what the game wrote.* The [JavaScript page](../reference/javascript.md#arrow-functions-and-the-conditional-operator) explains each part.

Although the instruction also lowers the enemies' health, the hook only acts on **its target**: the player's Health address, resolved through the pointer chain at every write. Enemies still take full damage. The debug window shows it – select the hook, click **Debug**, and fight: the enemies' writes appear as skipped, with the reason "writes another address".

!!! warning "Why the pointer chain matters here"
    Without a pointer chain, a hook recognises its target after a restart by the *callers* that wrote it (see [caller learning](../guide/hooks.md#after-a-restart)). Here that cannot work: player and enemies are hurt through the same call chain (`ApplyDamage → TakeDamage`), so the callers are the same. Give Health a pointer chain before relying on this hook across restarts.

!!! example "Variations"
    - **Never below 1 health:** template **Clamp**, minimum `1`. The player can still be hit, but not killed.
    - **No damage at all:** template **Fixed value** on the `TakeDamage` row, with your maximum health as value. Resting and level-ups still work, because they are other instructions.

## Method hooks

A method hook does not need the write watch. It catches a whole method, and its script sees the method's arguments by name. For HermesQuest the right place for anything about damage is `Combat.CalculateDamage`: every hit of everyone goes through it, and its result is the damage that will be dealt.

### Find the method and watch it

1. **View → Catalog …**, type `CalculateDamage` into the filter.
2. Select the method `CalculateDamage` of the class `Combat` – its parameters show as `(Character,Character,single)`, `single` being C#'s name for `float` – and click **Monitor**.
3. Fight a little. The method monitor lists every call with its arguments – `attacker`, `target`, `baseDamage` – and the result.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Method monitor](../assets/screenshots/method-monitor-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The method monitor shows each call with its object, arguments, result and caller (here in another Mono game).</figcaption>
</figure>

Select the method in the monitor and click **Create hook …**. The dialog asks for a template and for **When** the script runs:

- **After the call: change the result** – the script sees `ctx.result` and can return a new one.
- **Before the call: change arguments and fields** – the script can change `ctx.args` and objects before the method uses them.

### Everyone hits twice as hard

Template **Result × factor**, factor `2`, after the call. Every damage, of the player and of the enemies, is doubled. The message log still shows `x1 x1` as multipliers, but the damage dealt is doubled; the F1 view marks the result as changed.

That is rarely what you want. The next step makes the hook tell attacker and target apart.

### Only the player hits harder, and takes less

Template **Method script**, after the call, with this code:

```js
// After Combat.CalculateDamage: ctx.result is the damage it computed.
if (ctx.args.attacker.IsPlayer)
  return ctx.result * 3;      // the player deals three times the damage
if (ctx.args.target.IsPlayer)
  return ctx.result / 2;      // and takes half
// no return: every other hit stays as it is
```

Line by line:

- `ctx.args.attacker` is the method's first argument, a `Character` object. `.IsPlayer` reads its field `IsPlayer` from the game's memory – `true` or `false`.
- `return ctx.result * 3` ends the script and replaces the method's result. The game then deals that damage.
- If neither condition holds, the script ends without `return`, and the game keeps its own result.

Lines starting with `//` are comments and change nothing.

### God mode, the right way: before the call

Suppose you want the player to take no damage at all. A hook *after* `Character.TakeDamage` comes too late: that method has already lowered `Stats.Health` when it returns; its result is only the health lost. So hook it **before the call** and change its argument:

Method `TakeDamage (single)` of `Character`, template **Method script**, **Before the call**:

```js
// Before Character.TakeDamage(amount): ctx.this is the character hit.
if (ctx.this.IsPlayer)
  ctx.args.amount = 0;
```

- `ctx.this` is the object the method runs on – here the `Character` being hit.
- `ctx.args.amount = 0` changes the argument before the method sees it. `TakeDamage` then subtracts 0.
- Enemies are hit normally, because for them `IsPlayer` is `false`.

The message log now reports 0 damage for hits on the player, next to the base damage that would have hit. Your own hits on enemies count in full.

### Double experience

Method `AddExperience (double)` of `Character`, **Method script**, before the call:

```js
if (ctx.this.IsPlayer)
  ctx.args.amount = ctx.args.amount * 2;
```

Kill a goblin: instead of 10.25 the player gains 20.5 experience, and level-ups come twice as fast – the game's own `LevelUp` runs as usual, because the hook changed what `AddExperience` received, not the stored value.

For `AddGold (int)` the same idea needs whole numbers, because the parameter is an `int`:

```js
ctx.args.amount = Math.round(ctx.args.amount * 1.5);
```

## Value hook or method hook?

| Goal | Better |
| --- | --- |
| Multiply, fix or clamp one value | Value hook – simplest, and works in any game |
| Treat player and enemies differently | Method hook on `CalculateDamage` or `TakeDamage`, checking `IsPlayer` |
| Change what a method works with (its arguments) | Method hook, before the call |
| Survive a new game without a pointer chain | Method hook – it catches the method, whichever objects it is called for |

Both kinds are stored per program and reinstalled the next time you attach to HermesQuest. They can be paused, debugged and removed in the **Hooks** tab.

```

`docs/examples/hermesquest-scans.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: scans and pointer scan

Start [HermesQuest](index.md), attach to it with **Select process** (`HermesQuest.x86_64`, or `HermesQuest.exe` under Wine/Proton) and keep the **F1** view of the game at hand: it shows every value exactly.

The [scanning guide](../guide/scanning.md) explains the scan types; here they are applied to a game whose values behave like those of real games.

## Gold: an exact integer

Gold starts at 0, and searching for 0 finds millions of addresses. So earn some first:

1. Press **2** to spawn a goblin and walk into it until it dies. The log says how much gold it dropped, e.g. "You gain 10.25 experience and 5 gold."
2. In Grembyte choose the data type `int32`, scan type **Exact value**, enter the gold (`5`) and click **First scan**.
3. Kill another enemy, enter the new amount and click **Next scan**. After two or three rounds one address is left.
4. **Track** it and call it "Gold".

!!! tip "Why `int32`?"
    `Gold` is declared as `int` in the game's C# code, which is always 4 bytes. If you don't know the type, **Guess automatically** tries `int32`, `int64`, `float` and `double` at once.

## Mana: a float that changes on its own

Mana is a `float` that regenerates by 0.13 per second in real time. Between two scans it changes, even if you do nothing – exactly what makes values like stamina or energy bars hard to find in real games.

1. Spawn a rat (**1**) next to you and press **F**: Fire Bolt costs 7.5 mana. The panel beside the map shows mana with one decimal place, e.g. `MP 42.5/50`.
2. Data type `float`, **Exact value** `42.5`, float comparison **Rounded**. "Rounded" finds every value that shows as 42.5 with one decimal place (42.45 to 42.55), whatever the hidden decimals are. With **Exact** you would only find it within the same frame.
3. Spawn another rat and cast again. Scan **Decreased by …** `7.5` with tolerance `0.5`: the tolerance absorbs the mana that regenerated between the two scans. Don't wait long between casting and scanning – 0.5 mana regenerate in under four seconds.
4. Wait a few seconds and scan **Increased** – only mana grows by itself.
5. Track the address and call it "Mana".

Tracked, the value visibly counts up in the address list until it reaches 50.

## Experience: a double

`Experience` is a `double` (8 bytes). Enemies bring uneven amounts: a rat 4.5, a goblin 10.25, a skeleton 15.5.

1. Data type `double`, **Exact value** with the experience the F1 view shows, e.g. `14.75`.
2. Kill a skeleton (**3**), then **Increased by …** `15.5`, without tolerance: whole kills are exact.

!!! question "Why does `float` not find it?"
    A `double` and a `float` with the same value have entirely different bytes. A scan with the wrong type finds nothing – or, for small integers, chance hits. When a value shows decimals that don't fit, try the other floating-point type.

## Pointer scan: surviving "New game"

Press **N**: the game builds a new player, and all tracked addresses now point into memory the game no longer uses. A **pointer chain** finds the value again. Mana is a good target, because you can find it again right after a new game.

1. Right-click "Mana" → **Find pointers …**.
2. Look at **Chains start in**. In a Unity game the program file is only a small launcher. With the game's assemblies marked under **Assemblies** (e.g. `Assembly-CSharp`), **Marked assemblies** is ticked: chains start in the static fields of its C# classes. Without, **Engine modules** is: they start in the Mono runtime (`libmonobdwgc-2.0.so`, or `mono-2.0-bdwgc.dll` on Windows) or in `UnityPlayer`, and there are many more of them.
3. Click **New scan**. It finds many candidates.
4. Press **N** in the game. Find mana again as above: spawn a rat, cast, **Exact value** `42.5` rounded, then **Decreased by …** `7.5` ± `0.5`.
5. In the pointer dialog click **Take from scan**, then **Filter with this address**. Chains that only matched by chance drop out.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 once or twice. Then pick the shortest remaining chain and click **Use pointer**.

From now on "Mana" resolves after every new game and every restart of HermesQuest.

!!! tip "How to read a chain"
    The game reaches mana as `GameState.Current → Player → Stats → Mana`. The last offsets of a good chain are exactly these steps: the offset of `Player` in `GameState`, of `Stats` in `Character` and of `Mana` in `CharacterStats`. The object inspector shows each field's offset (see [Unity (Mono)](../engines/unity-mono.md)), so you can check a chain against the game's own structure. What comes before is the way from the Mono runtime to the static field `GameState.Current`.

!!! note "No chain found?"
    Raise **Max. depth** by one or two. Managed games often need deeper chains than native ones, because the way to a static field leads through the runtime's own tables.

With the chain in place you can give **Gold** and **Experience** chains too: they differ from Mana's only in the last offset, because all three are fields of the same `CharacterStats` object. Grembyte does not derive them for you: scan for each, then filter its pointer scan as above.

## A shortcut for Mono games

For scripts and method hooks you need no pointer chain at all: they reach the player through the game's own static field, `GameState.Current`, which is always right – see [Scripts](hermesquest-scripts.md). Pointer chains matter for tracked addresses, freezing and value hooks.

```

`docs/examples/hermesquest-scripts.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest: scripts

[Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) are JavaScript that Grembyte runs on the game's main thread, by hand or on a timer. They read and change the game's objects through their fields and call its methods – no addresses, no pointer chains. This page builds up from reading one value to scripts with parameters. If JavaScript is new to you, keep [JavaScript in Grembyte](../reference/javascript.md) open beside it.

To create a script: attach to HermesQuest, open the **Scripts** tab, click **New …**, give it a name, choose **When** it runs, and type the code. **Run now** runs the selected script at once; what it logs and returns appears in the log below the scripts.

## The way in: `GameState.Current`

In a Unity game, `ctx.find("ClassName")` finds Unity objects – GameObjects and components. HermesQuest keeps its state in plain C# objects, which Unity does not know about. Their entry point is a **static field**: `GameState.Current`, the running game. `ctx.static` reads it:

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
```

`"HermesQuest.GameState.Current"` is namespace, class and field. The result is an object you can walk through like in C#: `game.Player` is the player, `game.Player.Stats` its stats. Because the script asks for `GameState.Current` every time it runs, it always finds the current game – also after "New game", where tracked addresses need a pointer chain.

## 1. Show the character

**When:** Only when run by hand.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
const player = game.Player;
const stats = player.Stats;

ctx.log(`Level ${stats.Level}, turn ${game.Turn}, ${game.Kills} kills`);
ctx.log(`Health ${stats.Health.toFixed(1)} / ${stats.MaxHealth}`);
ctx.log(`Mana   ${stats.Mana.toFixed(1)} / ${stats.MaxMana}`);
ctx.log(`Gold   ${stats.Gold}, experience ${stats.Experience}`);

return player;
```

- `const` gives a value a name for the rest of the script.
- Text in backticks `` `…` `` is a *template*: `${…}` inserts a value. `toFixed(1)` rounds a number to one decimal place for display.
- `ctx.log(…)` writes a line to the script log.
- `return player` makes the player the script's result. The log shows it as a link: click it to open the player in the **object inspector**, with all its fields.

## 2. Heal fully – two ways

**When:** Only when run by hand.

Writing the fields directly:

```js
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
stats.Health = stats.MaxHealth;
stats.Mana = stats.MaxMana;
```

Assigning to a field (`stats.Health = …`) writes the new value straight into the game's memory. The game does not notice that anything happened.

Calling the game's own method:

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const healed = player.Heal(1000);
return `Healed ${healed.toFixed(1)} health`;
```

`player.Heal(1000)` runs the game's method `Character.Heal` with the argument 1000. That method follows the game's rules – it never heals above the maximum – and returns how much it healed, which the script shows as its result.

!!! tip "Field or method?"
    Writing a field is direct and works for every value. Calling a method lets the game do the work with its own rules: limits, side effects, messages. When the game has a method for what you want, prefer it.

## 3. Regenerate on a timer

**When:** Repeatedly, every 5 seconds.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
if (game === null || game.GameOver)
  return;

const healed = game.Player.Heal(1);
if (healed > 0)
  ctx.log(`+${healed} health`);
```

- `if (…) return;` ends this run early: before the first game exists (`null`) or when the player is dead.
- `||` means *or*. `game.GameOver` is a `bool` field of the game.
- Logging only when something happened keeps the log readable – a repeating script runs hundreds of times.

The next run starts five seconds after the previous one *ended*, so runs never overlap.

## 4. Stronger player, kept after "New game"

**When:** Repeatedly, every 2 seconds. **Parameters:** two numbers, `outgoing` (default `2`) and `incoming` (default `0.5`).

`Combat.CalculateDamage` multiplies every hit by the attacker's `DamageOutgoingMultiplier` and the target's `DamageIncomingMultiplier`. Setting them on the player is the game's own way to make it stronger – but "New game" creates a new player with both back at 1. A repeating script puts them back:

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const wanted = { DamageOutgoingMultiplier: ctx.args.outgoing,
                 DamageIncomingMultiplier: ctx.args.incoming };

for (const [field, value] of Object.entries(wanted)) {
  if (Math.abs(player[field] - value) > 0.0001) {
    player[field] = value;
    ctx.log(`${field} set to ${value}`);
  }
}
```

- `ctx.args.outgoing` is the value of the parameter `outgoing`. A timed run uses the parameter's default; **Run now** asks for the values.
- `{ name: value, … }` is a JavaScript object; `Object.entries` turns it into pairs, and `for (const [field, value] of …)` walks through them.
- `player[field]` is the same as `player.DamageOutgoingMultiplier` when `field` holds that name: square brackets take the field's name from a variable.
- `Math.abs(a - b) > 0.0001` compares floating-point numbers. The game stores `float`, JavaScript calculates with `double`; a value like 0.3 is not exactly equal in both, so `!==` would report a difference every time.

The message log of the game shows the multipliers in every hit, e.g. `(base 5 x2 x1)`.

## 5. Gold on demand

**When:** Only when run by hand. **Parameter:** a number `amount`, default `100`.

```js
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
const amount = Math.trunc(ctx.args.amount);
player.AddGold(amount);
return `${amount} gold added, now ${player.Stats.Gold}`;
```

`AddGold` takes an `int`; `Math.trunc` cuts off decimals someone may have typed. Run it with **Run now**: Grembyte asks for the amount first.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="560" }
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-light.webp#only-light){ width="560" }
  <figcaption>A manual run asks for the script's parameters (here a script of another game).</figcaption>
</figure>

## 6. Train an attribute – a choice parameter

**When:** Only when run by hand. **Parameters:** a choice `attribute` and a number `points` (default `1`).

The choice gets its options from a short piece of code. For `attribute`:

```js
return [
  { label: "Strength (melee damage)", value: "Strength" },
  { label: "Dexterity (hit chance)", value: "Dexterity" },
  { label: "Intelligence (Fire Bolt damage)", value: "Intelligence" },
];
```

The list shows the labels; the script gets the value. The script:

```js
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
const name = ctx.args.attribute;          // "Strength", "Dexterity" or "Intelligence"
const before = stats[name];
stats[name] = before + Math.trunc(ctx.args.points);
return `${name}: ${before} → ${stats[name]}`;
```

The options code runs in the game too, so it could also read them from it – for example the names of the enemies around. Here a fixed list is enough.

## 7. The nearest enemy

**When:** Only when run by hand.

```js
const game = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current");
const player = game.Player;
const enemy = game.NearestEnemy(player, 8);
if (enemy === null)
  return "No enemy within 8 steps";

const chance = ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", player, enemy);
ctx.log(`${enemy.Name}: ${enemy.Stats.Health} health, hit chance ${Math.round(chance * 100)} %`);

enemy.Stats.Health = 1;
return enemy;
```

- `game.NearestEnemy(player, 8)` calls a method of the game object and passes the player object along; the game returns a `Character` or `null`.
- `ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", …)` calls a **static** method – one that belongs to a class, not to an object. The name is written as the catalog shows it: `Namespace.Class:Method`.
- `enemy.Stats.Health = 1` leaves the enemy at one health point; the next hit kills it.

## 8. Remember between runs: `ctx.state`

**When:** Repeatedly, every 10 seconds.

```js
const gold = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats.Gold;

if (ctx.state.lastGold !== undefined && gold > ctx.state.lastGold)
  ctx.log(`+${gold - ctx.state.lastGold} gold in the last 10 seconds`);

ctx.state.lastGold = gold;
```

Variables declared with `const` exist for one run only. `ctx.state` is an object that the script keeps while Grembyte stays attached, also when you edit the code: whatever the script stores in it is there again on the next run. On the first run `ctx.state.lastGold` does not exist yet – it is `undefined` – which the `if` checks before comparing.

## When something goes wrong

- **An error** stops the run and appears in the log with its message, e.g. for a misspelt field: *HermesQuest.CharacterStats has no field Helth*. The script stays and runs again at its next time.
- **`null`**: before the game has created its state, or for an enemy that is gone, a field or method returns `null`. Check with `if (x === null)` before using it.
- **Names are case-sensitive**: `stats.health` is not `stats.Health`. The object inspector (open it from a returned object) shows the exact names.
- **Long loops freeze the game**: a script runs on the game's main thread, and the game waits until it ends. Keep scripts short and never write a loop that waits for something in the game – use a repeating script instead (its interval must be above 0).

```

`docs/examples/index.md`:

```md
# HermesQuest

HermesQuest is a small role-playing game made for trying out Grembyte. It is a Unity game with the Mono backend, so every tool works on it: value scans, pointer scans, the write watch, value hooks, and the [Unity (Mono)](../engines/unity-mono.md) tools – catalog, trace, method monitor, method hooks and scripts. The first three examples use it; the [next two](#examples-with-the-test-game) use the small C test game of the tutorial, and [one](#examples-in-other-games) a released game.

It is deliberately built like a real game: the values live in heap objects behind pointers, "New game" moves them to new addresses, player and enemies share one class, and all damage goes through one pipeline that hooks and scripts can change.

## Download

| System | Download |
| --- | --- |
| Linux (native, x86-64) | [HermesQuest-RPG-Linux](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Linux) |
| Windows, or Linux under Wine/Proton | [HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/releases/download/v0.5.0-alpha/HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip) |

Both are zip archives with the game folder in them. The Linux file has no `.zip` extension, but unpacks the same way.

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    unzip HermesQuest-RPG-Linux -d HermesQuest
    ./HermesQuest/Linux/HermesQuest.x86_64
    ```

    In Grembyte the game shows up as `HermesQuest.x86_64`. Remember the [permissions](../getting-started/permissions.md): with `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` at `1`, Grembyte cannot reach a game it did not start.

=== "Windows"

    Unpack `HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip` and start `Windows\HermesQuest.exe`. In Grembyte it shows up as `HermesQuest.exe`.

=== "Under Wine/Proton"

    The Windows build is also the test case for [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md):

    ```bash
    unzip HermesQuest-RPG-Windows.zip -d HermesQuest
    wine ./HermesQuest/Windows/HermesQuest.exe
    ```

    or add `HermesQuest.exe` to Steam as a non-Steam game and start it with Proton. The first time you select it, Grembyte offers to download Frida's Windows gadget.

`-seed <n>` on the command line fixes the map and every roll, also after "New game", so a run can be repeated exactly:

```bash
./HermesQuest/Linux/HermesQuest.x86_64 -seed 42
```

## Playing

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrows, WASD, numpad | Move; walk into an enemy to attack it |
| Space / R | Wait / rest (recover 2 health) |
| F | Fire Bolt at the nearest enemy, costs 7.5 mana |
| E, 1–5 | Spawn a random enemy / a rat, goblin, skeleton, orc or ogre |
| Delete | Remove all enemies |
| C | Character sheet |
| F1 | Debug view with the exact values and the process ID |
| H | Help |
| N | New game |

Enemies only appear when you spawn them, so you decide when a fight starts. Killing one brings experience and gold:

| Enemy | Key | Health | Experience | Gold |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rat | 1 | 6 | 4.5 | 0–2 |
| Goblin | 2 | 12 | 10.25 | 3–8 |
| Skeleton | 3 | 18 | 15.5 | 2–10 |
| Orc | 4 | 28 | 24.75 | 8–20 |
| Ogre | 5 | 60 | 60 | 20–45 |

The **F1** view shows every value with all its decimal places – handy to check what a scan should find – and the process ID to pick the right process in Grembyte.

## How the game is built

This is what the examples rely on. All code is in the namespace `HermesQuest`; the catalog shows it in the assembly `Assembly-CSharp`.

### The values

```text
GameState.Current            static field: the running game
  └─ Player                  Character
       ├─ Stats              CharacterStats
       │    ├─ Level         int
       │    ├─ Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence   int
       │    ├─ Health, MaxHealth                   float
       │    ├─ Mana, MaxMana                       float
       │    ├─ Experience                          double
       │    └─ Gold                                int
       ├─ DamageOutgoingMultiplier                 float, 1.0
       └─ DamageIncomingMultiplier                 float, 1.0
```

- The player starts with 50 health, 50 mana, 0 experience and 0 gold.
- **Mana regenerates by 0.13 per second** in real time, also while the game is in the background. A value that changes on its own is a good test for scans with tolerance.
- **Experience is a double** with decimals (a goblin brings 10.25), shown rounded on the character sheet.
- **New game** builds a new `GameState` with a new player and new stats: all addresses change, as after loading a save game in a real game.

### The damage pipeline

Melee attacks and Fire Bolt, of the player and of enemies, all go through the same methods:

```text
Combat.MeleeAttack / Combat.CastFireBolt
  └─ Combat.ApplyDamage(game, attacker, target, baseDamage, source)
       ├─ Combat.CalculateDamage(attacker, target, baseDamage)
       │      returns baseDamage × attacker.DamageOutgoingMultiplier
       │                         × target.DamageIncomingMultiplier
       └─ Character.TakeDamage(amount)      writes target.Stats.Health
```

- Player and enemies are both `Character`; `IsPlayer` tells them apart. A hook on `TakeDamage` therefore hits everyone unless it checks `IsPlayer`.
- The message log shows base damage and multipliers of every hit, and the F1 view the last calculation, so you see at once what a hook or script changed.
- Every method that writes a value has a method of its own: `TakeDamage`, `Heal`, `SpendMana`, `RegenerateMana`, `AddGold`, `AddExperience`. They are compiled without inlining, so each is a separate function in memory that the write watch names and that a hook can catch.

## The examples

1. [Scans and pointer scan](hermesquest-scans.md): find gold, mana and experience, and a pointer chain that survives a new game.
2. [Hooks](hermesquest-hooks.md): multiply gold at the instruction that writes it, protect the player but not the enemies, change damage with method hooks.
3. [Scripts](hermesquest-scripts.md): read and change the character from JavaScript, heal on a timer, scripts with parameters.

## Examples with the test game

The native tools need a game without an engine adapter. These examples use the C test game of the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md) (`test_app/dummy_game.c`):

1. [Code explorer](dummy-game-code-explorer.md): from a button's text to the function that pays out gold, and a native script that gives 500 gold through it.
2. [Pointer chain from the code](dummy-game-pointer-chain.md): find the pointer chain to the gold by reading the code that changes it, instead of with a pointer scan.

## Examples in other games

- [Underkeep: a hidden debug menu](underkeep-debug-menu.md): two native scripts open a debug menu in a game with an engine of its own, under Proton.

If JavaScript is new to you, [JavaScript in Grembyte](../reference/javascript.md) in the reference explains the language as far as hooks and scripts need it, along these examples.

If you have never used Grembyte, do the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md) with the small C test game first; it explains the main window step by step.

`docs/examples/underkeep-debug-menu.md`:
