# Underkeep: a hidden debug menu

Underkeep runs on an engine of its own under Proton, so there is no engine adapter: this example uses [scripts in native games](../guide/scripts.md#scripts-in-native-games), which find code by its bytes. It needs the [code explorer](../guide/code-explorer.md) to follow along, and no other preparation.

Underkeep (own engine, under Proton) has a hidden debug menu. Two native scripts make it usable: the first opens the menu, the second switches on the commands behind its buttons.

```js title="Open the hidden debug menu (Underkeep, own engine, under Proton)"
const n = ctx.native;
// OpenPage(int page, bool replace): push rbp / sub rsp, 0x20 / cmp [menu], 0 / mov ebp, ecx / je
const openPageAt = n.scan("40 55 48 83 EC 20 83 3D ?? ?? ?? ?? 00 8B E9 0F 84");
// The cmp at +6 reads the menu object: +0 state (0: closed), +4 page
const menu = n.rip(openPageAt.add(6), 2, 7);
if (menu.readS32() === 0) return "Open the in-game menu first (Esc)";
n.fn(openPageAt, "void", ["int", "uint8"])(11, 0);
return "Debug menu opened";
```

The menu opens, but its buttons do nothing yet. Each button sends a console command (`heal_party`, `kill_nearby_enemies`, …), and each command first asks a check that in the release build only logs *"This command is available only in debug mode."* and returns false. The [code explorer](../guide/code-explorer.md#from-a-string-to-the-code) leads there from that message. A second script patches the check so that it returns true (`mov al, 1; ret`); run again, it restores the original bytes:

```js title="Switch the debug commands on or off (Underkeep, own engine, under Proton)"
const n = ctx.native;
// The check: push rbx / sub rsp, 0x50 / mov ebx, -1 / lea rdx, [message] / … /
// xor al, al / add rsp, 0x50 / pop rbx / ret. The first three bytes are left
// open: they are what this script changes.
const check = n.scan(
  "?? ?? ?? 83 EC 50 BB FF FF FF FF 48 8D 15 ?? ?? ?? ?? 44 8B C3 48 8D 4C 24 30 " +
  "E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 45 33 C9 48 C7 44 24 20 00 00 00 00 45 33 C0 48 8D 54 24 30 " +
  "8D 4B 02 E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 48 8B 44 24 30 48 85 C0 74 13 F0 0F C1 18 83 FB 01 " +
  "75 0A 48 8B 4C 24 30 E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? 32 C0 48 83 C4 50 5B C3");
const ORIGINAL = [0x40, 0x53, 0x48];  // push rbx / (sub rsp …)
const ALLOW = [0xB0, 0x01, 0xC3];     // mov al, 1 / ret
const now = Array.from(new Uint8Array(check.readByteArray(3)));
const is = bytes => bytes.every((value, i) => value === now[i]);
if (!is(ORIGINAL) && !is(ALLOW))
  throw new Error(`unexpected bytes at ${check}: ${now.map(b => b.toString(16)).join(" ")}`);
const allow = is(ORIGINAL);
Memory.patchCode(check, 3, code => code.writeByteArray(allow ? ALLOW : ORIGINAL));
return allow ? "Debug commands enabled" : "Debug commands disabled again";
```

To use the debug menu:

1. Attach Grembyte to the game and add both scripts in the **Scripts** tab, each set to *Only when run by hand*.
2. Run **Switch the debug commands on or off** once. The result says *Debug commands enabled*.
3. In the game, open the in-game menu with ++esc++, then run **Open the hidden debug menu**. Page 11 of the menu appears: kill nearby or all enemies, level up the party, unlock skills, 100 skill points, heal the party, reveal the map, unlock all recipes and fast travel, weather, and more.
4. The buttons now work. To switch the commands off again, run the second script once more.

The patch lives only in the game's memory: restarting the game undoes it, and the scripts must be run again. Both were found in version 1.0.4; their byte patterns keep them working as long as an update leaves the two functions alone.

!!! warning "Achievements and statistics"
    The debug commands include `reset_steam_stats_and_achievements`, which resets your Steam statistics and achievements. Achievements may also still unlock while the commands are enabled.

<small>Underkeep is named on this page only to illustrate how Grembyte works. All game names, trademarks and game content belong to their respective owners. Grembyte is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by them.</small>

```

`docs/getting-started/first-hook.md`:

```md
# Tutorial: your first hook

This tutorial uses the small test game in the repository to go through the whole path once: find the gold, see which code changes it, and hook that code so every gold gain is ten times as large. It takes about ten minutes.

## The test game

`test_app/dummy_game.c` is a minimal GTK game with buttons for **Gold +100**, **Gold −100** and **New game**, plus mana, experience and a treasure hunt for trying [fuzzy scans](../guide/scanning.md#fuzzy-scans). As in real games, the player lives on the heap behind pointers (`g_game → player → gold`), so the address of the gold changes with every start and every **New game**. The game prints its PID, the pointer chain and the current address of the gold to the terminal, so you can check what Grembyte finds. Several instances may run at once.

Build and start it (needs `gcc` and the GTK 3 development packages: `gtk3-devel` on Fedora, `libgtk-3-dev` on Debian/Ubuntu):

```bash
mkdir -p build
gcc -O2 test_app/dummy_game.c -o build/dummy_game.exe $(pkg-config --cflags --libs gtk+-3.0)
./build/dummy_game.exe
```

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Grembyte next to the test game](../assets/photos/dummy-game-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Grembyte next to the test game](../assets/photos/dummy-game-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Where this tutorial leads: the test game on the right, Grembyte on the left with its gold found and tracked through a pointer chain.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 1. Attach to the game

Click **Select process** in Grembyte and choose `dummy_game.exe`. The toolbar and the status bar now show the program, its PID and whether it is 32 or 64 bit.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Process selection](../assets/screenshots/process-list-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Process selection](../assets/screenshots/process-list-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption>Select process lists the running programs; Wine/Proton games appear as their Windows program.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 2. Find the gold

1. Enter the gold shown in the game as **Search value**, keep the data type `int32` and click **First scan**. Thousands of addresses hold that number by chance.
2. Click **Gold +100** in the game, enter the new value and click **Next scan**. Repeat until one or a few addresses are left.
3. Select the address and click **Track** (or double-click it). Give it a description such as "Gold".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Main window after scanning](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Main window after scanning](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>After two scans three addresses are left; the gold is tracked below.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 3. See which code writes it

Right-click "Gold" in the tracked addresses and choose **Address watch (writes)**. Click **Gold +100** in the game: the watch window lists the code location that raised the gold, e.g. `dummy_game.exe+0x…`. **Gold −100** produces a second row of its own.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The write watch lists each code location that wrote the gold, how often, and whether it reads or writes the value.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 4. Hook it

Select the row of the increase and click **Create hook …**. Choose the template **Multiplier**, factor `10`, and "Increases only".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Create hook dialog](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Create hook dialog](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
  <figcaption>The hook dialog builds its form from the parameters of the chosen template.</figcaption>
</figure>

The hook appears in the **Hooks** tab. Every click on **Gold +100** now brings 1000 gold; the column **Last** shows the old value → the value the game wrote ⇒ the value stored.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Active hooks with their template, target and last call.</figcaption>
</figure>

In the **Hooks** tab hooks can be edited, paused, debugged and removed. When a hook is removed, when you select another process and when Grembyte exits, the original bytes of the game are restored.

## 5. Make it last

Restart the game, or click **New game**: the gold now lives at another address. For the tracked address and the hook to find it again, give "Gold" a pointer chain with the [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md). From then on both follow the gold after every restart, and Grembyte installs the hook again by itself whenever you attach to the game.

## Where next

- [Scanning](../guide/scanning.md) explains every scan type, including tolerance and rounded floats with the game's mana and experience.
- [Hooks](../guide/hooks.md) explains how a hook works, what happens after a restart, and its limitations.
- [Hook templates](../guide/templates.md) shows how to write manipulations of your own in JavaScript.

```

`docs/getting-started/installation.md`:

```md
# Installation

## Get the source code

Grembyte is not offered as a ready-made installer. You download its source code from GitHub and install it with Python, as described further down. GitHub is a website where software projects keep their files; you need no account to download them.

The project page is **<https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte>**. There are two ways to get the files from it:

- **Download a ZIP file**: no extra programs, a few clicks in the browser. Good for trying Grembyte out. For a newer version you download the ZIP again.
- **Clone with Git**: needs the program Git once, then a single command brings your copy up to date. Recommended if you want to follow the development.

Either way you end up with a folder with the project's files, the **project directory**. All later commands on this page run in it.

!!! tip "Pick a simple place"
    Put the project directory somewhere you will find it again and whose path has no spaces or special characters, for example `~/Programs/grembyte` on Linux or `C:\Programs\grembyte` on Windows. The menu entry and shortcut installed below point to this folder, so it should stay there.

### Option 1: Download as a ZIP file

1. Open <https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte> in your browser.
2. Above the list of files, click the green **Code** button.
3. In the menu that opens, click **Download ZIP** at the bottom. The browser saves a file named `grembyte-main.zip`, usually in your *Downloads* folder.
4. Extract the ZIP file:
    - **Linux**: right-click the file in your file manager and choose *Extract here* (the wording depends on the desktop), or in a terminal: `unzip grembyte-main.zip`
    - **Windows**: right-click the file in Explorer, choose **Extract All…**, and confirm.
5. This creates a folder `grembyte-main`. Move it to the place you picked and rename it to `grembyte` if you like. This folder is your project directory.

!!! note "Do not start from inside the ZIP"
    Windows lets you open a ZIP file like a folder. Always extract it first; programs cannot run properly from inside the ZIP.

**Updating:** download the ZIP again, extract it and replace the old project directory with the new one. Then repeat the [install](#install) step, because the virtual environment `.venv` lives in the project directory. Your addresses, hooks, scripts and settings are not affected: Grembyte keeps them outside the project directory (see [Files and environment](../reference/files.md)).

### Option 2: Clone with Git

Git is a program that downloads a project and later fetches only the changes. *Cloning* means making your own local copy of the project.

**Install Git** (once):

=== "Linux"

    Git usually comes from the distribution's package manager. Check first whether it is already there:

    ```bash
    git --version
    ```

    If the command is not found, install it:

    ```bash
    sudo apt install git     # Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint
    sudo dnf install git     # Fedora
    sudo pacman -S git       # Arch, Manjaro, SteamOS desktop mode
    ```

=== "Windows"

    Download Git for Windows from <https://git-scm.com/downloads/win> and run the installer. The default settings on every page are fine; just click **Next** through to **Install**.

    Alternatively, in a terminal with `winget`:

    ```powershell
    winget install --id Git.Git -e
    ```

    Afterwards open a **new** terminal (PowerShell or *Terminal* from the Start menu) and check that it worked with `git --version`.

**Clone the project:**

Open a terminal (Linux: e.g. *Konsole* or *Terminal*; Windows: *PowerShell* or *Terminal*), change to the folder that should contain the project directory, and clone:

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    mkdir -p ~/Programs
    cd ~/Programs
    git clone https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte.git
    cd grembyte
    ```

=== "Windows"

    ```powershell
    mkdir C:\Programs -Force
    cd C:\Programs
    git clone https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte.git
    cd grembyte
    ```

`git clone` creates the folder `grembyte` with all files; that is your project directory. The last command already takes you into it, so you can continue straight with the [install](#install).

**Updating:** in the project directory run

```bash
git pull
```

This fetches the latest changes. If they changed the dependencies, running `python -m pip install -e .` again with the virtual environment activated brings them up to date; it does no harm if nothing changed.

!!! note "Changed files"
    `git pull` refuses to overwrite files in the project directory you edited yourself. If you did not mean to change them, `git status` lists them and `git restore <file>` puts a file back. Your Grembyte data is not in the project directory and is never touched by Git.

## Requirements

- GNU/Linux or Windows on x86-64
- Python 3.11 or newer, with `venv` and `pip`
- On Linux a graphical session with X11 or Wayland

The Python dependencies, PySide6 (Qt) among them, are installed with `pip` from `pyproject.toml` into the virtual environment; Qt itself comes with PySide6. What has to come from the system is Python and, on Linux, a few X11/XCB libraries that Qt's `xcb` platform plugin loads. Desktop installations usually have most of them, but `libxcb-cursor` is often missing, and Qt 6 needs it for the `xcb` plugin.

### System packages on Linux

=== "Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint"

    ```bash
    sudo apt update
    sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip
    sudo apt install libxcb-cursor0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-icccm4 libxcb-image0 \
        libxcb-keysyms1 libxcb-randr0 libxcb-render-util0 libxcb-shape0 libxcb-xkb1 \
        libegl1 libgl1 libfontconfig1 libdbus-1-3
    ```

=== "Fedora"

    ```bash
    sudo dnf install python3 python3-pip
    sudo dnf install xcb-util-cursor xcb-util-wm xcb-util-image xcb-util-keysyms \
        xcb-util-renderutil libxkbcommon-x11 mesa-libEGL mesa-libGL fontconfig dbus-libs
    ```

=== "Arch, Manjaro"

    ```bash
    sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip
    sudo pacman -S --needed xcb-util-cursor xcb-util-wm xcb-util-image xcb-util-keysyms \
        xcb-util-renderutil libxkbcommon-x11 libglvnd fontconfig dbus
    ```

=== "openSUSE"

    ```bash
    sudo zypper install python3 python3-pip
    sudo zypper install libxcb-cursor0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-icccm4 libxcb-image0 \
        libxcb-keysyms1 libxcb-randr0 libxcb-render-util0 libxcb-shape0 libxcb-xkb1 \
        libEGL1 libGL1 fontconfig libdbus-1-3
    ```

    On Leap the default `python3` can be older than 3.11; install a newer one, e.g. `python311`, and create the virtual environment with `python3.11 -m venv .venv`.

On a Wayland session Qt uses its `wayland` plugin, whose libraries every Wayland desktop already has. The XCB packages are still worth installing: Qt falls back to `xcb` (through XWayland) when the Wayland plugin cannot start. If Grembyte still does not start, see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

### For Windows games under Wine or Proton

Grembyte builds a small Windows helper the first time a Wine/Proton game needs it (see [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md#loading-the-gadget)). It needs MinGW, the compilers `x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc` and `i686-w64-mingw32-gcc`:

| System | Packages |
| --- | --- |
| Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint | `gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64 gcc-mingw-w64-i686` |
| Fedora | `mingw64-gcc mingw32-gcc` |
| Arch, Manjaro | `mingw-w64-gcc` |
| openSUSE | `mingw64-cross-gcc mingw32-cross-gcc` |

Without MinGW it uses zig instead: `./.venv/bin/pip install ziglang` installs it into Grembyte's virtual environment, where the build finds it.

On Windows nothing besides Python is needed: install it from <https://www.python.org/downloads/windows/> (tick *Add python.exe to PATH*) or with `winget install --id Python.Python.3.13 -e`.

### Supported platforms

**Tested**: Grembyte is developed on these systems, and every release is tried on them:

| System | Version | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fedora Linux | 44 | KDE Plasma on Wayland, Python 3.14; native games and Windows games under Wine/Proton |
| Windows | 11 26H2 | |

**Expected to work, not tested**: these meet the requirements above, but nobody checks them regularly. Problems specific to them may go unnoticed until someone reports them:

| System | Version | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debian | 12 and newer | Python 3.11 from the distribution |
| Ubuntu, Linux Mint | Ubuntu 24.04 / Mint 22 and newer | Ubuntu 22.04 ships Python 3.10, which is too old |
| Arch Linux, Manjaro | current | |
| openSUSE | Tumbleweed; Leap with Python 3.11 or newer | |
| Other Linux distributions | | with Python 3.11+ and the libraries above |
| Windows | 10 22H2 | |

**Not supported**: macOS, 32-bit systems and ARM computers (Grembyte reads x86 and x86-64 code).

If Grembyte runs on a system that is not tested, or does not, a [bug report](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/issues) or a short note helps.

## Install

In the project directory:

=== "Linux"

    ```bash
    python3 -m venv .venv
    source .venv/bin/activate
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    python -m pip install -e .
    ```

=== "Windows"

    ```powershell
    py -m venv .venv
    .venv\Scripts\activate
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    python -m pip install -e .
    ```

The editable install also sets up the console command `grembyte`.

## Start

With the virtual environment activated:

```bash
grembyte
```

Or straight from the project directory, without activating anything:

```bash
./.venv/bin/python -m grembyte
```

### Menu entry and shortcut

=== "Linux"

    `scripts/grembyte.sh` activates the virtual environment (`.venv` in the project, or `$GREMBYTE_VENV`) and starts Grembyte from any working directory. A menu entry for the current user (KDE, GNOME, …) appears under Development and Games:

    ```bash
    ./scripts/install-desktop-entry.sh              # install or update the entry
    ./scripts/install-desktop-entry.sh --uninstall  # remove it
    ```

    The entry points to the project directory, so run the script again after moving the repository.

=== "Windows"

    `scripts\grembyte.cmd` starts Grembyte the same way. For the Start menu and the taskbar, install a shortcut for the current user, then right-click "Grembyte" in the Start menu and choose "Pin to taskbar":

    ```powershell
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows-shortcut.ps1             # install or update
    powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install-windows-shortcut.ps1 -Uninstall  # remove it
    ```

## Language

The interface is German or English, depending on the system locale (English for any other locale). Choose it under [Settings → General …](../guide/settings.md), or for one start with `GREMBYTE_LANGUAGE=en` or `de` (see [environment variables](../reference/files.md)).

## First start

At the first start Grembyte creates its SQLite database, where it keeps addresses, hooks, templates, scripts and settings per game. [Files and environment](../reference/files.md) lists where it lives and how to move it.

On Linux, continue with the [permissions](permissions.md) Grembyte needs to read another process's memory.

## Troubleshooting

### A Python module is missing

```text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'PySide6'
```

(or `frida`, `capstone`, `sqlalchemy`, `grembyte`, …) almost always means that Python runs outside the virtual environment, or that the install step did not finish.

1. Check which Python runs. With the environment activated, the path must end in the project's `.venv`:

    ```bash
    python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
    ```

    If it does not, activate it (`source .venv/bin/activate`, on Windows `.venv\Scripts\activate`) or start Grembyte with `./.venv/bin/python -m grembyte`. The menu entry and the shortcut use `.venv` by themselves.

2. Install again and read the end of the output; an error there names the package that failed:

    ```bash
    python -m pip install -e .
    ```

3. Check the dependencies:

    ```bash
    python -m pip check
    python -c "import PySide6, frida, capstone, psutil, numpy, sqlalchemy; print('ok')"
    ```

A failed `pip install` usually comes from a Python that is too old (`python --version`, at least 3.11) or a version so new that a package has no prebuilt wheel for it yet. Then create the environment with an older Python, e.g. `python3.13 -m venv .venv`, after deleting the old `.venv`. After moving the project directory, also delete `.venv` and install again: a virtual environment does not survive being moved.

### Qt cannot load a platform plugin

```text
qt.qpa.plugin: From 6.5.0, xcb-cursor0 or libxcb-cursor0 is needed to load the Qt xcb platform plugin.
qt.qpa.plugin: Could not load the Qt platform plugin "xcb" in "" even though it was found.
This application failed to start because no Qt platform plugin could be initialized.
```

The plugin is there, but a system library it needs is missing. Install the [system packages](#system-packages-on-linux) for your distribution first. If that does not help:

1. Let Qt report what fails:

    ```bash
    QT_DEBUG_PLUGINS=1 grembyte
    ```

    The output names the plugin and the library that could not be loaded (`Cannot load library …: libxcb-cursor.so.0: cannot open shared object file`).

2. List every library of the `xcb` plugin that is not found:

    ```bash
    ldd .venv/lib/python3*/site-packages/PySide6/Qt/plugins/platforms/libqxcb.so | grep "not found"
    ```

    Search your package manager for the missing file name, e.g. `dnf provides '*/libxcb-cursor.so.0'`, `apt-file search libxcb-cursor.so.0` or `pacman -F libxcb-cursor.so.0`.

3. Try the other platform plugin. On Wayland, `wayland` and `xcb` are both possible:

    ```bash
    QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland grembyte
    QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb grembyte
    ```

    Remove a `QT_QPA_PLATFORM` set in your shell profile or environment that names a plugin your session does not have.

A message `Could not find the Qt platform plugin "…" in ""` (*find*, not *load*) means that PySide6 itself is incomplete: install it again with `python -m pip install --force-reinstall PySide6-Essentials`.

If neither helps, open a [bug report](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/issues) with the output of `QT_DEBUG_PLUGINS=1 grembyte`, your distribution and its version.

```

`docs/getting-started/permissions.md`:

```md
# Permissions on Linux

Grembyte reads and changes the memory of a game that runs as your own user. Linux allows that only to a process that may *trace* the game: the same check that applies to debuggers such as gdb. Yama's `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope` decides who may:

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | A process may trace any other process of the same user. |
| `1` | Only its own child processes. The default of many distributions. Grembyte then cannot access a game started separately. |

## What needs which access

Grembyte uses three ways into a game, and each feature needs only one of them. All of them act on processes of your own user only; Grembyte needs no root rights and asks for none.

| Access | Used by | Needs `ptrace_scope = 0` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **None**: reading `/proc` and files | the process list, the [code explorer](../guide/code-explorer.md) (it reads the game's file on disk, not its memory), the offline catalog, settings and the database | no |
| **`/proc/<pid>/mem`**: reading and writing memory | [value scans](../guide/scanning.md), changing and freezing [addresses](../guide/addresses.md), the [pointer scan](../guide/pointer-scan.md), the [memory viewer](../guide/tools.md#memory-viewer) | yes |
| **[Frida](https://frida.re)**: an agent in the game | the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) and [hooks](../guide/hooks.md) with the Frida backend, the [native trace and monitor](../guide/native-tools.md), [scripts](../guide/scripts.md), and all [engine tools](../engines/index.md): catalog, trace, method monitor, object inspector, method hooks, calling methods, call graph, GAS attributes | yes, for native Linux games (Frida loads its agent through ptrace) |
| **ptrace** directly, like gdb | the write watch and hooks with the [ptrace backend](../guide/write-watch.md#backends-frida-or-ptrace) (CPU debug registers, nothing is injected); for Wine/Proton games a fallback to load the Frida gadget | yes |

Scans and the address list therefore need `ptrace_scope = 0` as much as the Frida tools do; only the process list and the code explorer work without it. Grembyte starts nothing in the game on its own: Frida and ptrace are only used when you open one of the tools above, and the game is released when you close it or detach.

For **Wine and Proton games** Grembyte loads Frida's Windows gadget into the game instead, through a small Windows helper; ptrace serves only as a fallback. The gadget listens on `127.0.0.1` only and is checked against its published checksum; see [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md#the-frida-gadget).

Grembyte makes no other network connections, apart from links you open yourself (documentation, bug reports).

## Allowing access for a session

Games started through [grembyte-cli](../guide/launch-option.md#permissions) are its children, so their saved hooks and scripts work with `ptrace_scope = 1` as well. Do not run Grembyte as root just in case, and do not loosen `ptrace_scope` permanently system-wide. For a session a temporary change is enough; it lapses at the next reboot. Note down the current value first, so you can restore it later:

```bash
sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope        # show the current value, e.g. 1
sudo sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0
```

!!! warning "This is a system-wide setting"
    `ptrace_scope` is not a setting of Grembyte. It changes the ptrace policy for the whole system: as long as it is `0`, every process of your user may inspect and modify every other process of that user, not just Grembyte and the game. Restore the previous value once you are done.

To undo the change without rebooting, set the value you noted before (on most distributions `1`):

```bash
sudo sysctl kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1
```

A reboot also restores the distribution's default, unless the value was set persistently in a file under `/etc/sysctl.d/`. In that case remove or change the entry there and reload it with `sudo sysctl --system`.

The process list only shows processes whose information the current user may access.

## One Grembyte per game

Each Grembyte process brings its own Frida agent into the game, and two agents hook the same functions of the game. Two Grembyte windows attached to the same game, or Grembyte and another Frida tool, can crash it. For native Linux games Grembyte therefore refuses to attach while another program's Frida agent is in the game; close the other Grembyte or Frida tool first. Under Proton it cannot tell, so make sure only one is attached. [grembyte-cli](../guide/launch-option.md#taking-the-game-over-in-the-window) is the exception: the window takes the game over from it.

## Windows

On Windows no extra permissions are needed for games running as the same user.

```

`docs/guide/addresses.md`:

```md
# Tracked addresses

The **Tracked addresses** tab keeps the addresses you work with, with a description, the type, the live value and, if found, a pointer chain. They are stored per program and loaded again the next time you attach to it.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Tracked addresses](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Tracked addresses](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Addresses with pointer chains (purple) resolve again after a restart; "HP" is frozen at 100.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Adding addresses

- **Track** in the scan results, or a double-click on a result.
- **+ Address …** for an address you know, e.g. from another tool.
- **Pointer chain …** for a value reached through pointers, e.g. `game.exe+0x43E600 -> 0x28 -> 0x0`: start at an address in a module (`module+offset`, also with further offsets), then each step reads the pointer at the address so far and adds its offset. Separate the steps with `->`, `=>`, `:` or `→` (as the [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md) and the [code explorer](code-explorer.md#pseudocode) show chains). The dialog shows where the chain leads now; the entry follows it again with every refresh and after a restart.
- From the object inspector, the hooks tab and scripts, which can hand addresses over.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Adding a pointer chain](../assets/screenshots/pointer-chain-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Adding a pointer chain](../assets/screenshots/pointer-chain-dialog-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption><strong>Pointer chain …</strong> with the gold of the test game: below the input, where the chain leads now.</figcaption>
</figure>

!!! note "Plus or arrow"
    `game.exe+0x43E600+0xB0` is the address `0xB0` bytes behind `game.exe+0x43E600`. `game.exe+0x43E600 -> 0xB0` reads the pointer stored at `game.exe+0x43E600` and adds `0xB0` to it. If a register held the object's address itself (`rcx` = `game.exe+0x43E600`), its field is at the sum; only if the object's address was read from there is it an arrow.

!!! example "Step by step with the test game"
    The [pointer chain example](../examples/dummy-game-pointer-chain.md) reads the chain of the gold from the game's code, enters it with **Pointer chain …**, and explains with a simple picture how to tell a step of a chain from an offset.

Double-click the description to rename an entry. If an address lies in the program's static memory (a global variable), Grembyte stores it as module + offset right away; it stays valid after a restart without a pointer scan.

## Writing and freezing

**Write value** writes a new value into the game once.

**Freeze** holds the current value: Grembyte writes it back every 100 ms. Clicking again releases it; **Write value** changes the frozen value. For entries with a pointer chain or a static address the frozen state is stored and still applies after the game restarts. Entries without a chain are released when they are loaded again, because their address need no longer be right then.

!!! question "Freeze or hook?"
    Freezing needs no write watch and works on any value, but may flicker briefly, since the game can change the value between two passes. A [hook](hooks.md) with the template *Fixed value* acts directly at the write instruction, so the game never sees another value.

## Context menu

A right-click on an entry offers:

- **Show in memory viewer**: the [memory](tools.md#memory-viewer) around the address.
- **Change description …** and **Change value …**.
- **Address watch (writes)** and **Address watch (all accesses)**: the [write and read watch](write-watch.md).
- **Find pointers …**: the [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md); **Remove pointer** drops a chain again.

Scan results offer the memory viewer and the two watches as well.

## After a restart

Without a pointer chain the stored address is usually wrong after the game restarts, and the entry shows a stale value. With a chain Grembyte resolves it again; while it cannot (e.g. in the main menu, before a save is loaded) the address column shows `?`, and the entry resolves once the chain leads somewhere again.

```

`docs/guide/code-explorer.md`:

```md
# Code explorer

**View → Code explorer …** finds the code behind something the game shows or logs. It reads a module's file – the game's executable or one of its libraries, a PE image (also under Wine/Proton) or an ELF file – and lists its strings, the instructions that refer to them, its functions and their callers. Because it reads the file and not the game's memory, it cannot disturb the game, and it also works without a game attached (**Open file …**). x86 and x86-64 code is supported.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Code explorer](../assets/screenshots/code-explorer-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Code explorer](../assets/screenshots/code-explorer-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The test game: the button text "Find treasure" among the strings, the instruction in <code>on_activate</code> that hands its handler <code>on_treasure</code> to GTK, and <code>on_treasure</code> calling <code>add_gold</code>.</figcaption>
</figure>

!!! example "Step by step with the test game"
    The [code explorer example](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md) goes from the button **Find treasure** of the tutorial's test game to the function that pays out the gold, and ends with a native script that gives 500 gold through it.

It is the static counterpart of the [native trace and monitor](native-tools.md): the trace shows which functions run, the explorer shows what a function does and who calls it. A function found here can be [called from a script](scripts.md#scripts-in-native-games).

## From a string to the code

Most ways into unknown code start with a text: a menu entry, a message, a log line, a console command. New to assembly? The [assembly quick reference](../reference/assembly.md) explains what the disassembly shows.

1. Choose the **module**. The game's executable comes first, then the modules in its folder. Indexing a large executable takes a few seconds; the window keeps the result while Grembyte runs.
2. Type words of the text into the filter of the **Strings** tab and select the string. The references list shows every instruction that loads its address, with the function it is in.
3. Double-click a reference to open its **function**. Above the disassembly, the explorer shows the function's **signature guessed from its code** (x86-64): `void add_gold(int rdi)`, from the argument registers the function reads before writing them and from what its callers do with the result – see [how it is guessed](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md#4-what-add_gold-takes). The disassembly names what instructions refer to: strings, functions, imported functions of other modules (`SDL_PollEvent`, `kernel32.dll!CreateFileW`), and pointers to strings or functions.
4. **Callers** lists who calls the function. Double-click one to go there; **Back** returns.

### Pseudocode

The tab **Pseudocode (guess)** next to the disassembly shows the function as C-like code, at most one statement per instruction. The beginning of `refresh_ui` in the [test game](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md) reads:

```c
void refresh_ui(void)
{
    rbx = *(uint64_t *)(g_game + 0x28);     // 0x4007cc  g_game → 0x28
    eax = 0;                                // 0x4007d0
    snprintf(rsp, 0x100, "Gold: %d", *(int32_t *)rbx); // 0x4007d4  g_game → 0x28 → 0x0
    …
```

The comment after a statement holds the **address of its instruction**, in the code: it leads to the line in the disassembly, not to a value in memory. Where the statement reaches memory from a global, the comment adds the **pointer chain** to it, written as the [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md) writes it: `g_game → 0x28 → 0x0` is the pointer in `g_game`, plus `0x28`, the pointer read there, plus `0x0` – the gold. The chain stays valid when the game allocates a new player, an address read in the game does not.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Pseudocode of refresh_ui](../assets/screenshots/code-explorer-pseudocode-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Pseudocode of refresh_ui](../assets/screenshots/code-explorer-pseudocode-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption><code>refresh_ui</code> as pseudocode, at the instruction selected in the disassembly: the call of <code>snprintf</code> that reads the gold through <code>g_game → 0x28 → 0x0</code>. Above it the find bar, above that the callers of <code>refresh_ui</code>.</figcaption>
</figure>

- The head is the guessed signature. Arguments are called `a1`, `a2` … until their register is overwritten; all other values keep their register's name, so each line matches its instruction in the disassembly.
- Globals, strings, functions and read-only constants appear by name or value (`g_game`, `"clicked"`, `7.5f`) instead of `[rip + 0x2a31]`. A global without a name starts a chain as `module+0x…`.
- A value used only once, right after it is computed, is folded into that use: `rbx = *(uint64_t *)(g_game + 0x28)` instead of `rax = g_game;` and `rbx = *(uint64_t *)(rax + 0x28);`. A value read more than once, or read after a branch, stays in its register.
- Calls show their arguments and the register the caller reads the result from: `eax = rand();`, `add_gold(eax + 20);`. Arguments come from the assignments to argument registers just before the call (folded into it) and from the callee's guessed signature. Without either, a register stands for an argument; `...` means more may follow on the stack.
- Conditions come from the instruction that set the flags: `if (a1 <= 0) goto loc_…;`, unsigned comparisons with a cast, float comparisons as such. If a register the comparison read changes before the jump, the condition stays `/* flags of cmp … */`.
- Saving registers and the stack frame are left out; a jump to another function is a call followed by `return`.
- There are no loops or `if`/`else` blocks, only `goto`, and no variables beyond registers. Instructions it does not translate stay as `asm("…")`.

Switching tabs keeps the place: the pseudocode opens at the line of the instruction selected in the disassembly (or the next line, if that instruction has none of its own), and clicking a line of the pseudocode selects its instruction, so **Monitor**, **Copy pattern** and the other actions work from there. **Ctrl+F** finds a text in the pseudocode – a name, an address such as `0x4007e8`, an offset such as `0x14`; **Enter** and **Shift+Enter** go to the next and previous match.

It is a reading aid, not a decompiler: read it next to the disassembly, and check what matters there.

!!! example "Step by step: a pointer chain from the code"
    The [pointer chain example](../examples/dummy-game-pointer-chain.md) reads the chain of the test game's gold from `add_gold`, puts it on the address list so it survives **New game**, and explains how to tell a step of a chain from an offset.

!!! tip "Found by a write watch"
    The write watch lists the instruction *after* the write (**Trap PC after write**): the processor reports a write once the writing instruction has finished. The instruction that wrote is the one before it in the disassembly.

A string is not always loaded by the code directly. Tables of names (commands, settings) hold pointers to their strings; the explorer lists such a pointer as a reference of the kind *pointer*. Double-clicking it shows who reads that table entry.

**Go to** takes an address of the file (e.g. `0x140257270`), an address in the game's memory, `module+0x…`, or the name of an export or symbol. Code opens its function; data shows who refers to it. Double-clicking an instruction follows the address it refers to.

## Using what you found

| Button | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Copy pattern** | Copies the shortest unique byte pattern starting at the selected instruction (or the function's start). Addresses, branch targets and RIP-relative displacements become `??`, so the pattern still matches after an update that moved the code around. The status line says whether it is unique. |
| **Copy script** | Copies a [native script](scripts.md#scripts-in-native-games) that finds the selected instruction or function by that pattern. For a function it prepares a call with `ctx.native.fn`, with the arguments and return type guessed from the code; for an instruction loading an address it resolves that address (`ctx.native.rip`, or the absolute address in a 32-bit game). Paste it into a new script and adjust it. |
| **Monitor** | Logs the calls of the function, or the runs of the selected instruction, in the [native function monitor](native-tools.md#native-function-monitor). Needs the game attached. |
| **Memory** | Shows what the selected instruction refers to in the [memory viewer](tools.md#memory-viewer). Needs the game attached. |

## Symbol names

The explorer uses names wherever available: in the function list, references,
disassembly, pseudocode and **Go to**. ELF files supply their symbol tables;
PE files supply exports and imports. On Windows the folder button next to the
file (**Symbol folder**) reads the names from matching PDB files in a folder you
choose, through Windows' DbgHelp, and loads the module again.

### Names from the engine

IL2CPP and Unreal games compile their code ahead of time into a module the
explorer reads, and their engines know what that code is called. With the game
attached, **Engine names** asks the engine adapter and names the module's code:

- **IL2CPP:** every C# method in `GameAssembly` as `Namespace.Class:Method`.
  Code several methods share (identical code folded by the linker, shared
  generic code) is named after one of them, with the number of the others:
  `List:Clear [+12]`.
- **Unreal:** every native `UFunction`'s exec thunk as `Class::execName`, the
  wrapper Blueprint calls go through into C++. Blueprint functions run in the
  script interpreter and have no code of their own.

The names are added to the module loaded in the explorer and stay until it is
closed; names from the file (symbols, exports) keep priority. Mono games are
not covered: their C# code is compiled while the game runs and lies in no file.

### Class names from C++ RTTI

Polymorphic C++ classes keep their names in the file for `typeid` and
`dynamic_cast`, even in stripped builds without symbols. The explorer reads this
run-time type information (MSVC in PE files, GCC/Clang in ELF files) and names
each class's **vtable** and the **virtual methods** in it by their slot:
`CGameSprite::vftable`, `CGameSprite::vf12`. Underkeep's `underkeep.exe`, for
example, gives 163 classes this way.

- A method several classes share without overriding it keeps the name of the most
  basic class (the one with the shortest vtable).
- A function found in different slots (a shared stub such as `_purecall`, or
  identical code the linker folded together) gets no name.
- With multiple inheritance the further vtables are named by their offset in the
  object (`Both::vftable@0x10`); only the first one names methods.
- Template arguments are shown as `<…>`, so instances of a template share their name.
- Names from symbols, exports and PDBs take precedence.

## Limits

- Functions come from the executable's exception directory (64-bit PE), its symbols (ELF), its exports and the targets of calls; names from its symbols, exports, imports and C++ RTTI. Code reached only through tables of addresses may show no function; **Go to** still finds its references.
- The disassembly is a linear sweep: data inside the code section (jump tables) shows as odd instructions.
- Code a runtime compiles while the game runs is in no file and not in the explorer: the C# methods of Mono games (the write watch names them, e.g. `Scripts:GivePlayerMoney+0x61`), scripts of other virtual machines. For C# use the [catalog, the calls and the method monitor](../engines/unity-mono.md); IL2CPP games compile C# ahead of time into `GameAssembly`, which the explorer does read.
- Packed or encrypted executables (some copy protections) hold no readable code in their file.

```

`docs/guide/data.md`:

```md
# Saving, export and import

## What Grembyte keeps per game

Grembyte identifies a game by its program and keeps for it:

- tracked addresses with their pointer chains and frozen values,
- hooks and method hooks,
- scripts,
- [notes](notes.md) in Markdown,
- favorites and the chosen assemblies,
- catalogs read from Unity and Unreal games (in a cache in Grembyte's data folder, see [files](../reference/files.md)), so the catalog also opens offline.

Hook templates and settings are shared by all games. Everything lives in one SQLite database; [Files and environment](../reference/files.md) says where.

When the attached game exits, Grembyte resets the window within a second: scans, watches, freezing and hooks stop; stored addresses and hooks are kept and loaded again the next time you attach.

## Export and import

**File → Export game data …** writes everything saved for a game to a JSON file: per program path its addresses, hooks, method hooks, favorites, scripts and notes, plus the templates its hooks were created from. The candidate chains of pointer scans are only exported when you ask for them, since they can be large.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Export](../assets/screenshots/game-export-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Export](../assets/screenshots/game-export-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

**File → Import game data …** puts the entries of a file into one saved program, whatever path they were exported from – useful when a game moved, or for another computer. It either replaces what the program holds or mixes the file's entries in, leaving out those it holds already. A template in the file is linked to a local one with the same name and code, otherwise added (under a new name if the name is taken).

Notes are never deleted by an import, not even by **Replace**: a note of the file is merged into the program's note: the parts of its text between lines (`---`) that the note does not hold yet are appended below such a line. A program without notes takes them as they are.

## Where exports go

Every export – game data, the [bug report](tools.md#log-and-activity), a text from the text viewer, an object saved from the [object inspector](../engines/index.md#object-inspector) – starts in the folder you saved the last one to. The first time that is your home folder, on Windows your documents folder.

## Cleaning up

- **File → Delete saved entries …** deletes chosen addresses, pointer scans, hooks, method hooks, favorites, scripts or notes of saved programs, or the programs altogether. Tick the entries per program; the box in front of a row ticks all its entries. For several selected rows (Ctrl or Shift), the space key ticks their entries, a second time their program too, a third time nothing. Deleting an address deletes its pointer scans as well. **Remove process** deletes the program with all its entries and its assembly selection; it is saved anew when you attach to it again.
- **File → Compact database …** frees the space of deleted entries (e.g. large pointer scans) that SQLite otherwise keeps in the file.
- **Obsolete pointer scans** are offered for deletion after the start: scans whose filtering left no candidates, scans of entries with a pointer that were not filtered for 7 days, and scans not filtered for 60 days. Untick the ones to keep; they are offered again only after they were filtered or scanned anew. Grembyte compacts the database afterwards. Pointer scans are stored compressed; scans of older versions are converted once at the first start.

```

`docs/guide/hooks.md`:

```md
# Hooks

A value hook changes writes to a target address: with the Frida backend it intercepts writes at a specific instruction; with `ptrace` it watches the address and corrects its value after each write. Hooks are stored per program and installed again the next time it starts.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hooks tab](../assets/screenshots/hooks-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The Hooks tab with its log below the table.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Creating a hook

1. Find the instruction that writes the value with the [write watch](write-watch.md).
2. Select its row and click **Create hook …**.
3. Give it a **Description**, e.g. *Gold*: it names the hook in the table and in the messages of [grembyte-cli](launch-option.md).
4. Choose a [template](templates.md) and fill in its parameters. The built-in ones are **Multiplier**, **Fixed value** and **Clamp**.

The top of the dialog names the target: its address and type, and the write site, the code location as `module+offset`. A hook created from a tracked address with a [pointer chain](pointer-scan.md) follows the chain.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Create hook](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Create hook](../assets/screenshots/hook-dialog-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

Further options in the dialog:

**Caller levels**
:   For hooks without a pointer chain: how many return addresses identify a caller that writes the target (default `1`, at most `4`, `off` learns no callers). See [after a restart](#after-a-restart).

**Install as**
:   With the Frida backend: **Jump in the code (fast)** writes a jump to the hook into the game's code. **Hardware breakpoint (code unchanged)** leaves the code as it is and uses one of the CPU's debug registers to stop at the write instruction instead (at most three at a time). Useful where code must not change; some anti-tamper protections detect debug registers, though. This is different from the `ptrace` backend, which watches the target data address.

## The Hooks tab

Several hooks can be selected at once (Ctrl/Shift-click): **Pause**, **Debug** and **Remove** act on all of them, **Edit** on one. The columns:

- **Address**: the target – an address, the pointer chain it follows (`↳ …`), *dynamic · N callers* for a hook that changes only the writes of its learned callers, or *dynamic (all writes)* for one that changes every write of its code location. Method hooks show *C# method*.
- **Status**: *Active*, *Paused*, *Training* (waiting for a write, see [after a restart](#after-a-restart)), *Failed* (could not be installed), *Script error* (its script threw), *Removed by game* (the game restored or replaced the code at the write site, see [limitations](#limitations)) or *Disconnected* (its session ended).
- **Applied**: how often the hook ran. With **Hooks: measure their cost** in the [settings](settings.md), its tooltip adds calls per second, skipped writes and the time they cost.
- **Last (old → game ⇒ new)**: the last call as old value → value written by the game ⇒ value stored.

Below the table a log shows what hook scripts write with `ctx.log` or `console.log`, and the errors of hooks, also without debug mode; at most 100 lines per 0.1 s, more are counted as dropped.

For Frida hooks, when a hook is removed, when you select another process and when Grembyte exits, the original code bytes are restored. `ptrace` hooks do not patch game code.

## Debugging hooks

**Debug** puts the selected hooks into debug mode and opens the debug window. It logs every call with time, thread, address, caller, old value, game value, result, `ctx.log` output and errors with their stack. Writes the hook skips appear too, with the reason, such as "writes another address" or "caller not learned".

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hook debug window](../assets/screenshots/hook-debug-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hook debug window](../assets/screenshots/hook-debug-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

Debug mode costs time in the game; with very many calls the agent drops entries and only counts them. Closing the window ends debug mode.

## After a restart

Module-based hooks are stored per program as module + offset of the write instruction. When the program is attached again after a restart, Grembyte reinstalls them if the bytes at that location still match. If they changed, e.g. after a game update, the hook is not installed.

If the write instruction lies in no module – e.g. in Mono/Unity JIT code, which is generated anew and elsewhere at every start – it depends on the target:

- **With a pointer chain** the hook is stored with the bytes of the write instruction and the surrounding code. In Mono games it also remembers the C# method of the write: after a restart Mono compiles that method and the hook is installed in it right away. Otherwise, or if that fails, the hook is in **Training**: Grembyte watches the chain's target with a hardware watchpoint of its own and installs the hook at the first write from matching code. It takes effect from the next write on. The tooltip of the status column shows how many writes from other code were discarded. At most three hooks can train at a time; hooks installed as a hardware breakpoint take one of these three slots each.
- **JIT code without a pointer chain** cannot be stored as a value hook, because its write site and target cannot be found again after a restart.

The original target address is no longer valid after a restart. How the hook recognises the right writes depends on how it was created:

- **With a pointer chain**: the hook resolves the chain at every write and only acts on the address it leads to at that moment. This is the most reliable variant.
- **Without a pointer chain on a module-based write site**: while running, the hook learns the callers (with **Caller levels** `off` it learns none: "Callers are not learned"), i.e. the return addresses on the stack, that write the target address. After a restart it only acts on writes from these callers. More caller levels help when the player and other objects are changed through the same helper function. If a learned caller also writes other addresses, Grembyte points it out.

## How a hook works

### Frida backend

Grembyte replaces the write instruction with a jump to the hook, which runs right after the game's write and stores the result. Since the hook only works with the old and the new value, it does not matter how the game writes (`mov`, `add`, `sub` …). If the same instruction also writes other objects, e.g. the enemies' gold, the hook only acts on its target: the watched address, the address of its pointer chain or, after a restart without a chain, the learned callers. Several hooks can share a write instruction; they run in the order they were created.

The built-in templates cost a fraction of a microsecond per write. Scripts of your own, debug mode and caller learning run in JavaScript, one call at a time: a slow script can make the game drop frames. The [implementation notes](../development/implementation-notes.md#write-hooks) describe the details.

### ptrace backend

`ptrace` does not patch the write instruction. It sets a hardware data watchpoint on the target address. After the game stores a value, the thread stops; Grembyte reads the new value, runs the transform in its local JavaScript engine, and writes the result back before resuming the thread. The game's unmodified value is briefly present in memory.

This backend watches addresses rather than instructions: shared code is distinguished by the watched address, and a hook needs a fixed address or a pointer chain. It supports at most four distinct watched addresses and does not provide JIT training, caller learning or per-call hook debug events. See the [backend comparison](write-watch.md#backends-frida-or-ptrace).

## Limitations

- x86-64 code only.
- The write instruction and the bytes up to the length of a jump (5 bytes) are overwritten. If other code jumps into the middle of this range, the game crashes; Frida hooks and Cheat Engine's code injection carry the same risk.
- If the write sits in a tiny function with less than 5 bytes before the next one, the setting *Hooks: short jump in tight spots* overwrites only 2 bytes with a short jump to `int3` padding nearby. The padding is found by a heuristic; if it guesses wrong, the game crashes.
- If the connection to Grembyte breaks off unexpectedly while a hook is active, the game may crash.
- `int64` and `uint64` values are exact in manipulations only up to 2^53.
- Some games repair their code. The setting *Hooks: patch hooks the game removed again* reinstalls them (e.g. for Dark Souls III); see the [warning about anti-tamper systems](../index.md).

!!! tip "Hooks on methods"
    In Unity and Unreal games you can also hook a whole method instead of a single write: change its arguments, the fields of its object, or its result. See [method hooks](../engines/index.md#method-hooks).

```

`docs/guide/launch-option.md`:

```md
# Starting games with grembyte-cli

`grembyte-cli` starts a game and installs the hooks, method hooks and scripts Grembyte saved for it, without the window. You set a game up once in Grembyte, then play it through the launch option.

## Setting it up

1. Attach to the game in Grembyte and set up its [hooks](hooks.md), method hooks and [scripts](scripts.md). They are saved for the program, as always.
2. In Steam, open the game's **Properties → General → Launch options** and put `grembyte-cli` in front of `%command%`, with the full path of your installation:

    ```text
    /path/to/grembyte/.venv/bin/grembyte-cli %command%
    ```

3. Start the game from Steam.

`grembyte-cli` starts the command first, so the game runs whatever goes wrong in Grembyte. Among the processes the command starts it looks for the one with something saved for it. It waits a few seconds so the engine can load, then attaches. It ends when the command ends and exits with the command's exit code.

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--delay SECONDS` | How long to wait after the game was found before attaching (default 5). Raise it for games that load their engine slowly. |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show the options. |

Options go before `%command%`, for example `/path/to/grembyte-cli --delay 15 %command%`.

## What it installs

- **Hooks** and **method hooks**, as the hook panel restores them at attach. A hook that learns its callers or its C# method keeps them, as in the window.
- **Scripts** that run once or repeatedly, and manual scripts with a [hotkey](scripts.md#hotkeys): pressed in the game, it runs the script with the defaults of its parameters. Manual scripts without a hotkey are left out: only the window can run them.
- If a session ends while the game still runs, `grembyte-cli` starts it again up to three times.

Its messages go to the terminal (start Steam from a terminal to see them) and to `grembyte.log` (see [Files and environment](../reference/files.md)).

`grembyte-cli` never attaches to a game that ships EasyAntiCheat or BattlEye. The game then runs without Grembyte.

`grembyte-cli` runs on Linux only: it finds the game through `/proc`.

## Proton games

`grembyte-cli` loads the [Frida gadget](../wine-proton.md#the-frida-gadget) as the window does, but it never asks: if the matching gadget is missing and automatic downloads are off (the default), it reports that it could not attach, and the game runs without Grembyte. Attach to the game once in the window, which offers the download, or switch automatic downloads on in the [settings](settings.md). For 32-bit games it picks the ptrace backend for hooks by itself, as the window does (see [32-bit games](../wine-proton.md#32-bit-games)).

## Permissions

Since the game is a child of `grembyte-cli`, attaching also works with `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1`, as long as the game stays a descendant. If a launcher starts the game and then exits, the game is no longer a descendant. It then needs `ptrace_scope = 0`, as with the window (see [Permissions](../getting-started/permissions.md)).

## Taking the game over in the window

While `grembyte-cli` runs a game, the window can take the game over, for example to change a hook:

1. Open the process list. A game that runs through `grembyte-cli` is marked with a link icon. **Only grembyte-cli** next to the filter shows only these games.
2. Attach to it. Grembyte asks whether to take the game over from `grembyte-cli`.
3. Confirm. `grembyte-cli` removes its hooks and stops its sessions, then the window attaches and restores the saved hooks and scripts as usual.

If you decline, the window does not attach. Two sets of the same hooks in one game can crash it.

Once the window detaches, attaches to another process or is closed (also if it crashes), `grembyte-cli` attaches again and installs what is saved then, including your changes. Taking the game over needs `ptrace_scope = 0`: the game is no child of the window.

```

`docs/guide/native-tools.md`:

```md
# Native trace and monitor

When a game offers no engine metadata – or the logic you look for is plain C++ – the native tools work on machine code directly, for any engine.

## Native trace

**View → Native trace …** answers *which functions run when I do this?* It uses Frida's Stalker to count the functions the chosen threads call:

1. Choose the threads and modules to follow. Preselected are the threads active right now and the modules in the game's folder.
2. **Start following**: Stalker recompiles the code of these threads and counts every function call. System libraries run unchanged; only calls into them are counted.
3. Record a **baseline** while the game idles.
4. Record a **scenario** while doing the thing you are interested in, e.g. paying gold.
5. The functions that are new in the scenario, or called more often there, are the candidates. **Notable functions only** shows just these, **Game code only** hides calls into system libraries; the filters above the table narrow by name and [number of calls](../engines/index.md#trace) (`%3`). Below, the first calls per thread are listed in their exact order, without the functions of the baseline.

The game runs noticeably slower while it is followed. The native trace can be [docked](tools.md#docking-windows) at the bottom of the main window.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Native trace](../assets/screenshots/native-trace-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Native trace](../assets/screenshots/native-trace-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Candidates after a baseline and a scenario, with how often each ran.</figcaption>
</figure>

Candidates can be marked with ★ as [favorites](../engines/index.md#favorites) or handed to the monitor. A function found this way can be called from a [script](scripts.md#scripts-in-native-games) through `ctx.native`. The [code explorer](code-explorer.md) shows what it does and who calls it.

!!! warning
    Stalker rewrites the code of the traced threads while it runs. Grembyte asks before it starts, since this can slow down or, rarely, crash a game. Under [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md) the native trace is experimental and will probably make the game freeze or crash.

## Native function monitor

**Monitor native function …** logs the calls of one function: its arguments, the result and the caller. For pointer arguments it compares the memory behind them before and after the call, so you see what the function changed. The monitor can be [docked](tools.md#docking-windows) at the bottom of the main window.

| | Arguments | Floating-point arguments | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linux, x86-64 | `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9` | `xmm0`–`xmm7` | `rax`, or `xmm0` |
| Windows and Wine/Proton, x86-64 | `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, then the stack | `xmm0`–`xmm3` | `rax`, or `xmm0` |
| 32-bit programs | the stack; on Windows and Wine/Proton also `ecx` | the stack | `eax` |

These are the [calling conventions](../reference/assembly.md#calling-conventions); the first argument of a C++ method is `this`, the object it runs on. 32-bit Windows programs pass it in `ecx` (thiscall), so the monitor logs `ecx` first there, with the memory behind it compared like an argument's. The xmm registers appear in a call's details with both readings, as `float` and as `double`: which one is meant, the signature tells (below). Writes to memory that no argument points to are not visible.

For a function in a module whose file Grembyte can read (x86-64), the column **Signature (guessed)** shows which arguments the function's code reads and what callers do with its result, as the [code explorer](code-explorer.md) guesses them: `void (int rdi)` for a function taking one `int` and returning nothing. With **Guessed signature** ticked, the log shows only those arguments, typed (`int rdi=23`, `float xmm0=1.5`), a `float` or `double` result read from `xmm0`, and no result for a `void` function; unticked, it shows the raw argument registers and `rax`. The [example with the test game](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md#4-what-add_gold-takes) explains how the guess is made and how to check it.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Native monitor](../assets/screenshots/native-monitor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Native monitor](../assets/screenshots/native-monitor-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

Open it from a candidate of the native trace, from a favorite, or with a location you type in: an address (`0x55aa…`), `module+0x…` (stays the same across restarts) or a symbol name. Before **Add**:

- **Arguments:** how many arguments are read per call. More than the function has does no harm; the rest show random register contents.
- **Compare (bytes):** how many bytes behind each pointer argument are compared before and after the call; `0` turns the comparison off. More finds more fields but costs time for functions called often.
- The kind: **Function start** logs arguments, result, caller and the memory comparison; **Single instruction** only the registers at every pass, for a location inside a function, e.g. from the [write watch](write-watch.md). **Automatic** takes the function start where a symbol begins, else the instruction. Never monitor an address inside a function as a function start: that overwrites a local variable of the game. For such a location **Monitor enclosing function** monitors the function it lies in.

Both options apply to functions added afterwards. **Only calls with changes** shows only calls after which something changed behind a pointer argument. Beyond 200 calls a second, calls are only counted, so that the game stays playable.

```

```md
# Notes

While you work on a game you learn where things are: which class holds the gold, which instance the player is, which method adds experience or puts an item in the inventory. **View → Notes …** keeps that per game, in a small window you can dock beside the main window.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Notes](../assets/screenshots/game-notes-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Notes](../assets/screenshots/game-notes-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Notes on the test game, docked beside the scanner, in the preview.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Opening the notes of a game

- With a game attached, **View → Notes …** opens its notes.
- Without one, Grembyte first asks for the game: the list holds every game it has saved (a game is saved once Grembyte attaches to it), with the number of its notes. Double-click a game or choose **Open notes**. This way you can read and add to your notes while the game is not running.
- If another game is attached while the notes are open, they switch to it automatically; what you wrote for the previous one is saved first. If that fails, Grembyte asks whether to discard the changes; otherwise the notes stay with the previous game.
- With the notes open, **View → Notes …** again switches them to the attached (or chosen) game.

Like a program's other entries, the notes belong to one program path: a game started under two Proton versions has two sets of notes (see [What Grembyte keeps per game](data.md#what-grembyte-keeps-per-game)).

## Writing

The window has two tabs:

- **Write** – the text in Markdown, a few characters that format it: `## Gold` is a heading, `- ` starts a list, `` `AddGold(int)` `` marks code. The [Markdown reference](../reference/markdown.md) lists what the preview understands.
  While you type, the Markdown is colored: headings bold, the formatting characters (`#`, `*`, backticks) dimmed, code and links in their own color. Code blocks marked `js`, `ts` or `json` are colored as JavaScript, `c` or `cpp` as C (see [Code](../reference/markdown.md#code)). The colors follow the theme.
- **Preview** – the text formatted, as on GitHub: headings, lists, tables, code, task lists with check boxes, in the colors of the theme (code blocks colored like in the Write tab, shaded table headers). Links open in your browser.

Grembyte saves the notes

- about two seconds after you stop typing,
- when you click **Save** or press ++ctrl+s++ (this always saves, even when nothing changed),
- when the window closes (also with ++esc++), when it switches to another game, and when Grembyte quits.

The text beside the buttons says whether there are unsaved changes or when the notes were saved last. If the notes cannot be saved (for example because the database is locked), closing the window asks whether to discard the changes; **Cancel** keeps it open with your text.

## Docking

**Pin to main window** docks the notes as a tab at the right of the main window, **Detach** gives them a window of their own again; the next time they open the same way (see [Docking windows](tools.md#docking-windows)). Unlike the game's tools, the notes stay open when the game ends or another program is chosen.

## What to write down

Notes are free text; a layout that works well:

```markdown
## Gold
- Class `PlayerInventory`, field `gold` (int)
- `PlayerInventory:AddGold (int)` – call it from a script, see script *Gold*

## Experience
- `CharacterStats:AddExperience (int, bool)`, second argument `false`

## Items
- `Inventory:AddItem (ItemDefinition, int)`, items from `GameDatabase.items`

## Open
- [ ] What resets the stamina?
```

Names of classes, methods and fields can be copied from the [catalog](../engines/index.md#catalog) and the [object inspector](../engines/index.md#object-inspector) (context menu **Copy cell** or **Copy row**).

## Export, import and deleting

The notes are part of a game's [export](data.md#export-and-import). An import never deletes notes, not even with **Replace**: the file's text is merged into the program's note. Its parts between lines (`---`) that the note does not hold yet are appended, each below such a line. So notes passed back and forth between two computers do not grow, and a line you wrote yourself is no problem. **File → Delete saved entries …** has a column for the notes (see [Cleaning up](data.md#cleaning-up)).

`docs/guide/object-browser.md`:

```md
# Object browser

The [object inspector](../engines/index.md#object-inspector) shows one object, but you first need that object: from a monitored call, a script result or a field of another object. The object browser starts from the other end. It lists the objects that live in the game right now, grouped by class, so you can open the player, the game state or a party member's inventory without knowing where they are kept.

It is available for [Unreal Engine](#unreal-engine) and [Unity Mono](#unity-mono) games. Open it with **View → Object browser …** while Grembyte is attached to the game.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Object browser](../assets/screenshots/object-browser-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Object browser](../assets/screenshots/object-browser-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The game's own classes in Pillars of Eternity, with the objects of <code>Health</code> opened.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The tree

The first level lists the classes that have live objects, with how many objects of exactly that class live (objects of subclasses count for their own class). Open a class to list its objects:

- Unreal objects and Unity objects show with their name, as `"Companion_Eder(Clone)_0"@0x2a41c80a1e0`.
- Strings show with their text.
- Other C# objects show as `Class@address`.

Games keep hundreds of thousands of objects, so a class's objects are only read when you open it, and a class lists at most 5,000 of them. The filter narrows them.

Double-click an object, or select it and click **Open in inspector**, to show its fields in the [object inspector](../engines/index.md#object-inspector). The context menu copies an object's address or name, or a class's name or address.

Objects live only for a while: a level, a fight, a session. To keep an interesting one for later, use **Save as HTML …** in its inspector. The page records its fields and getters as they were then.

## Narrowing the list

- **Package:** all packages, **Game only** (without the engine's and the framework's), or one package. A package is an assembly in Unity games (`Assembly-CSharp`) and a package as the catalog groups them in Unreal games (`/Script/<Module>`, `/Game/<Folder>`). The dropdown shows how many objects each one has.
- **Filter:** a class whose name contains all the words you type shows with all its objects. A class with objects named so shows with only those, e.g. `eder` finds `Health` with its object `Companion_Eder(Clone)_0`. The column *Objects* then shows those named so out of all.
- **Singletons only:** classes with exactly one object. The *Singleton* column says why: the engine class that has only one object (Unreal), the static field that holds it (Unity, e.g. `GameState.s_Instance`), or *one object* for a game class that just happens to have one.

The tree is a snapshot: objects created later are missing, and an object may be gone by the time you open it. **Refresh** reads the objects again.

Like the other tools that stay in use while you play, the object browser can be [docked](tools.md#docking-windows) beside the scanner. It closes when the game ends.

## Unreal Engine

Grembyte reads every object from the engine's object table (`GUObjectArray`), the same table [scripts](scripts.md) search with `ctx.find`. Reading it does not stop the game.

- The objects' names are `FName`s, which repeat: `PointsAvailableTracker` may exist once per widget. The tooltip of an object names its outer, the object it belongs to (`Sidekick in WidgetTree_7`).
- *Singletons* are objects of the engine's single-instance classes and their subclasses: game instance, subsystems, game mode, game state, player controller, world settings, game user settings.
- **Templates and reflection** also lists class default objects (`Default__…`), archetypes and the reflection objects themselves: packages, classes, functions, structs, enums. They are left out otherwise. The inspector shows a reflection object's properties, not its contents (an enum's values, a class's fields).

## Unity Mono

Grembyte reads the objects with Unity's own liveness calculation, the one Unity uses to unload unused assets. It finds the objects reachable from static fields and from Unity's objects.

- **The game stands still** while the calculation runs, since it marks every object it visits. The status line says for how long.
- **Objects only a thread's stack holds** are not found, e.g. a local variable of a method that is running right now.
- **Singletons** are found through static fields that hold a class's only object, also through generic bases such as `Singleton<T>`.
- Unity objects show with their name, which Grembyte asks Unity for on the game's main thread.
- **At most 2 million objects** are kept per read; the status line says when there were more. Some games keep far more alive (Vampire Survivors about 2.5 million, mostly JSON data), and the classes found last are then missing. [Settings](settings.md) → *Object browser: objects read* raises the limit to up to 10 million (16 bytes per object in the game).
- **Only one Grembyte per game** may be attached (see [permissions](../getting-started/permissions.md#one-grembyte-per-game)); two of them can crash it here.

It works from Unity 4 to Unity 6, in 64-bit and [32-bit games](../engines/unity-mono.md#32-bit-games), and also in games that [sleep out of focus](../engines/unity-mono.md#games-that-sleep-out-of-focus).

Tested in Pillars of Eternity (64-bit), Might & Magic X – Legacy (Unity 4.2, 32-bit, Proton) and Vampire Survivors (Unity 6, native Linux), where the newer API runs.

## Not yet available

- **Unity IL2CPP:** IL2CPP has its own liveness calculation (`il2cpp_unity_liveness_*`); the browser does not use it yet.
- **Native games:** without an engine's reflection there is no list of classes to group objects by.
