`docs/guide/pointer-scan.md`:

```md
# Pointer scan

Games keep most values on the heap, so their address changes with every start, every new game and often every level. What stays the same is the way there: a static pointer in the program, then a few offsets through the objects. The pointer scan finds these chains, e.g.

```
dummy_game.exe+0x4040 → 0x28 → 0x0
```

reads as: take the pointer at offset `0x4040` of the module `dummy_game.exe`, add `0x28` and read the pointer there, add `0x0` – that is the gold.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Pointer scan](../assets/screenshots/pointer-scan-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Pointer scan](../assets/screenshots/pointer-scan-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The pointer scan dialog with the chain of the test game and some chance hits.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Finding a chain

1. Right-click the tracked address → **Find pointers …** → **New scan**. In the test game it finds `dummy_game.exe+0x… → 0x28 → 0x0` (`g_game` → player → gold), plus some chance hits.
2. Make the value move: click **New game** (or restart the game) and find the value again in the scanner. The pointer dialog can stay open meanwhile; **Pin to main window** [docks](tools.md#docking-windows) it next to the scanner, as a tab beside other docked tools, and the next pointer scan opens there too until you click **Detach**. It stays open when the game ends.
3. Select the new result in the scanner, then **Take from scan** and **Filter with this address** in the pointer dialog. Chains that only matched because of the layout in memory drop out. A plain restart is often not enough for that, since the layout at start tends to be the same; a new game or a new level changes more.
4. Select the remaining chain → **Use pointer**.

From now on the tracked address resolves correctly after every restart, and hooks created from it follow the value too (see [hooks after a restart](hooks.md#after-a-restart)).

If the address lies in the program's static memory, no pointer scan is needed; the dialog says so, and **Use static address** puts it on the address list as it is.

## Search limits

| Field | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Max. depth | How many pointers a chain follows at most (1 to 7). More depth finds more but takes longer. | 5 |
| Max. offset | The largest distance between a pointer and the next target, i.e. how far into an object a field may lie | `0x1000` |

How many chains a scan keeps is set under **Settings → General … → Pointer scan** (**Max. results**, default 10 000), together with the thread stacks and the [alignment](#alignment); see [settings](settings.md#settings). Chains are collected shortest first. When the limit is reached, the dialog says so: chains of the deepest level found may be incomplete, deeper ones are missing. Raise the limit or lower the depth.

## Memory regions

The dialog sorts the program's writable memory into groups, each with its size; the tooltip lists the modules in it.

**Chains start in** the static memory of modules:

| Group | What it holds | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Main module | The program itself | on |
| Marked assemblies | Mono games: the static fields of the C# classes in the assemblies marked under **Assemblies** | on, once assemblies are marked |
| Game modules | Other modules in the game's folder | on |
| Engine modules | Engine runtimes and middleware: UnityPlayer, GameAssembly, Mono, Unreal's engine modules, PhysX, FMOD, Steam … | on, off once assemblies are marked |
| System modules | The system, Wine and the drivers: libc, ntdll, kernel32, Mesa … | off |
| Other modules | Everything else, e.g. Steam's overlay | off |

Between their steps chains pass through the heap, which is always searched. The thread stacks are searched only with **Search thread stacks** in the settings (off by default): stack contents change all the time; leaving them out gives fewer chance hits and a faster scan.

Turn on system or other modules only if no chain from the game's own modules survives a restart. The choice is kept for the next scan.

### Mono games: static fields as chain bases

In a Unity game with Mono, the program and its libraries hold hardly any of the game's data. The static fields of its C# classes, where singletons such as a game state keep their instance, lie on the heap: Mono gives each class a block of its own, which stays put while the game runs. Without them a chain has to find its way there through Mono's own tables, and since these point to each other in countless ways, a scan finds hundreds of thousands of candidates.

With the game's assemblies marked under **Assemblies**, **Marked assemblies** makes these blocks chain bases. The chains are few, short and readable, e.g.

```
[Assembly-CSharp] GameState.s_Instance → 0x5d0 → 0x1f0
```

After a restart of the game such an entry on the address list shows as not resolved until Grembyte has found the class's block again; a class the game has not used yet has none, and Grembyte keeps looking for it.

## Alignment

Two settings under **Settings → General … → Pointer scan** decide what counts as a pointer. Both default to the pointer size of the program (8 bytes in 64-bit, 4 bytes in 32-bit programs):

- **Pointers lie at** multiples of the pointer size, as compilers place them. Multiples of 4 also find pointers in packed structures of 64-bit programs (`#pragma pack`), but the scan reads twice as many values and finds more chance hits.
- **Pointers point to** multiples of the pointer size: real pointers to objects almost always are, numbers that merely look like an address usually are not. Multiples of 16 cut chance hits further; **any address** finds chains through a pointer into the middle of a structure (`&object->value`).

## Candidates

The chains found are saved for the entry as candidates, so they can still be filtered after the game was restarted.

The table lists the most promising candidates first, by their **Score**; its tooltip shows how it adds up:

| Feature | Points |
|---|---|
| Starts in the main module / a game module / an engine module | +40 / +30 / +20 |
| Chain length 1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 / 6 and more | +20 / +10 / 0 / −5 / −10 / −15 |
| All offsets up to 0x100 (else up to 0x400) | +10 (+5) |
| All pointers aligned: each points to the start of an object, not into its middle | +10 |

The score only sorts; whether a chain is stable shows when you filter after a restart. **Add all to address list** takes the best 500.

- **Add all to address list** adds every candidate as an entry of its own; after a restart the list shows which ones still lead to a sensible value. With several rows selected, the button reads **Add selected to address list** and adds only those.
- **Remove saved candidates** deletes them once a stable chain is in use. The entry and its pointer stay; a new scan finds candidates again.

A scan can take several megabytes in the database. **Use pointer** therefore offers to delete the candidates once they were filtered after a restart at least once (or right away for a static address). Scans left over are offered for deletion after the start of Grembyte; see [cleaning up](data.md#cleaning-up).

!!! example "The chain from the code instead"
    The code that uses a value often shows its chain, too: the [code explorer](code-explorer.md#pseudocode) writes it next to each line. The [pointer chain example](../examples/dummy-game-pointer-chain.md) reads the chain of the test game's gold from `add_gold` and enters it with **Pointer chain …** on the [address list](addresses.md#adding-addresses) – no scan needed.

!!! tip "Fewer, shorter chains"
    Prefer short chains from the game's own module over long ones through system libraries. When several chains survive filtering, keep the one with the fewest levels; repeat the filter step after a level change if in doubt.

```

`docs/guide/scanning.md`:

```md
# Scanning for values

The value search on the right of the main window finds the addresses where the game keeps a value. You narrow them down in steps: a **First scan** over the whole memory, then **Next scans** over the remaining results after the value changed in the game.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Value search](../assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Value search](../assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

## Data types

| Type | Size | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int8`, `uint8` | 1 byte | Flags, small counters |
| `int16`, `uint16` | 2 bytes | Older games, packed structures |
| `int32`, `uint32` | 4 bytes | The usual integer: gold, ammunition, levels |
| `int64`, `uint64` | 8 bytes | Large counters, money in some games |
| `float` | 4 bytes | Health, mana, positions, multipliers |
| `double` | 8 bytes | Experience, timers, values in managed games |

**Guess automatically** tries `int32`, `int64`, `float` and `double` at once. The smaller types match almost everywhere and have to be chosen explicitly.

By default the first scan skips addresses that are not a multiple of the type's size. Games almost always align their values, so the scan is faster and has fewer chance hits. To scan every address, turn off **Aligned addresses only** under [Settings → General … → Scan](settings.md#settings); it applies from the next first scan.

## Scan types

First scan:

| Scan type | Finds |
| --- | --- |
| Exact value | Addresses holding the value |
| Greater than / Less than | Values above or below the number |
| Between | Values between two numbers |
| Unknown initial value | Every address; useful when the game shows no number, e.g. a health bar |

Next scan, compared with the previous scan:

| Scan type | Keeps addresses whose value |
| --- | --- |
| Changed value / Unchanged value | changed or stayed the same |
| Increased (> last scan) / Decreased (< last scan) | went up or down |
| Increased by … / Decreased by … / Changed by … | changed by the given amount |
| Exact value, Greater than, Less than, Between | as in the first scan, against the current value |

!!! tip "Unknown values"
    For a health bar without a number: **Unknown initial value**, take damage, **Decreased**, wait, **Unchanged**, heal, **Increased** – a few rounds leave few addresses.

## Fuzzy scans

Games rarely show a value exactly as they store it. Two options help:

- **Tolerance (±)** for exact and by-X scans: `Increased by … 25` with tolerance `5` finds increases from 20 to 30.
- **Float comparison** for `float` and `double`: *Exact*, *Rounded* or *Truncated* to the decimal places you typed. `12.3` rounded finds 12.25 to 12.35.

The test game has examples of both:

- **Mana** (`float`, shown with one decimal place) regenerates by 0.13 every second; a spell costs 7.5. Scan **Exact value** with the value shown (e.g. `20.1`) and **Rounded**; with *Exact* the address is hard to find, because the stored value is e.g. 20.13. Then **Cast spell** and scan **Decreased by …** `7.5` with tolerance `0.5` – the regeneration between the scans would make a comparison without tolerance fail.
- **Experience** (`double`, shown without decimals): **Exact value** with the number shown and **Rounded**; after **Fight** scan **Increased by …** `12` with tolerance `3`.
- **Gold** (`int32`): after **Find treasure** scan **Increased by …** `25` with tolerance `5`.

## Taking results

Results show the address, type and live value. Select one or several and click **Track** (or double-click) to move them to the [tracked addresses](addresses.md). A right-click offers the memory viewer and the [write and read watch](write-watch.md) for a result directly.

The scan area folds away with **Hide address search** next to the tabs, **View → Address search** or ++ctrl+shift+f++; Grembyte remembers the choice.

```

`docs/guide/scripts.md`:

```md
# Scripts

Scripts are JavaScript function bodies that run on the game's main thread and can call its methods: give the player health every few seconds, set an attribute after loading, or run a cheat function by hand. They live in the **Scripts** tab next to **Hooks**, are stored per program and restored when that program is attached. **New …** and **Edit** open the script editor with the code, the schedule and the parameters.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Scripts tab](../assets/screenshots/scripts-tab-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Scripts tab](../assets/screenshots/scripts-tab-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>Scripts for an Unreal game with their schedule, and the script log below.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Run now** runs the selected script at once (asking for its parameters), **Pause** and **Resume** stop and restart its schedule, and **Remove** deletes it. The context menu also has **Create copy**. Below the table the script log shows what scripts write with `ctx.log` and what they return; **Inspect** behind a returned object opens it in the [object inspector](../engines/index.md#object-inspector), and **Clear** empties the log.

Scripts reach game objects and methods through the engine adapters of [Unity and Unreal games](../engines/index.md). In a game without an adapter – a native game with an engine of its own – they work on machine code instead: see [Scripts in native games](#scripts-in-native-games).

## When a script runs

| Mode | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| **Once, after a delay** | after the configured delay, each time the script starts |
| **Repeatedly, every …** | every configured interval; the next interval starts after the previous run finished, so runs do not overlap |
| **Only when run by hand** | only when you click **Run now**, or press its hotkey in the game |

### Hotkeys

A script that runs only by hand can have a **Hotkey**, for example ++ctrl+shift+g++. Pressed while the game has the focus, it runs the script with the defaults of its parameters, without asking. This also works when the game was started through [grembyte-cli](launch-option.md), with no window open. The table shows the hotkey next to *On request*.

- A hotkey is one key (a letter, a digit, ++f1++ to ++f12++, ++insert++, ++delete++, ++home++, ++end++, ++page-up++, ++page-down++, ++pause++ or ++space++) with any of ++ctrl++, ++shift++, ++alt++ and ++meta++. It fires once per press, only with exactly its modifiers: ++ctrl+g++ does not fire on ++ctrl+shift+g++.
- The game gets the keys as well; Grembyte only reads them. Pick a combination the game does not use.
- A paused script does not react to its hotkey.
- On Linux, Grembyte reads the keyboard through X11. Games under Wayland run through XWayland, so this covers native games and Proton alike. A game that is a Wayland client itself is not seen.

## Parameters

Scripts can have parameters of the types text, number, yes/no or choice. A manual run asks for their values; scheduled runs and hotkeys use their defaults. The script reads them from `ctx.args`.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="560" }
  ![Script parameters](../assets/screenshots/script-params-light.webp#only-light){ width="560" }
</figure>

A choice parameter gets its options from a short JavaScript function evaluated in the game, returning values or `{label, value}` objects. The list filters as you type; **Reload options** in the run dialog runs the options code again, e.g. after the game loaded more items. The [Unreal page](../engines/unreal.md#example-a-script-with-a-choice-parameter) shows one in Gothic 1 Remake.

## Writing scripts

The script's `ctx` gives access to the game; all fields are in the [script context reference](../reference/script-context.md). Objects of the game are [wrappers](../reference/script-context.md#object-wrappers): read and write their fields and properties and call their methods as in C# (`player.Heal(10)`). A returned object is shown as the result and can be opened in the object inspector.

```js title="Heal the player by 10 health (HermesQuest, Unity Mono)"
const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
return `Healed ${player.Heal(10).toFixed(1)} health`;
```

```js title="Keep an attribute at a value (Unreal, Gameplay Ability System)"
const might = ctx.gas.get("Might");
if (might && might.base < 14) ctx.gas.setBase("AttributeSetCore.Might", 14);
```

```js title="Count runs and remember state"
ctx.state.total = (ctx.state.total || 0) + 1;
ctx.log(`run ${ctx.runs + 1}, total ${ctx.state.total}`);
```

Scripts are different from [hook templates](templates.md): a template changes one value at one write, a script runs on its own and calls the game.

## Scripts in native games

Without an engine adapter Grembyte looks for a function the game calls every frame on its main thread, such as `SDL_PollEvent` or `SwapBuffers`, and runs scripts each time it returns. The first run logs which one it found. A game that exports none of the known ones, for example one with SDL linked in statically, gets an error instead.

There are no class or method names to go by, so `ctx.native` finds code by its bytes: a pattern of the function's first instructions, with `??` for the bytes that change between builds (addresses, offsets). A pattern survives game updates that leave the function alone, unlike a fixed address. The [code explorer](code-explorer.md) finds the code and copies its pattern, or a whole script skeleton. The [script context reference](../reference/script-context.md#native-code-ctxnative) lists the functions.

Native scripts run with Frida's full JavaScript API: memory is read and written through `NativePointer` (`pointer.add(4).readS32()`), and `Process`, `Module` and `Memory` are available as in any Frida script. A wrong call can crash the game: check a function's parameters in the disassembly first, and try the script by hand before giving it a timer.

An example with a real game: [Underkeep's hidden debug menu](../examples/underkeep-debug-menu.md), opened and made usable by two native scripts.

<small>Gothic 1 Remake is named on this page only to illustrate how Grembyte works. All game names, trademarks and game content belong to their respective owners. Grembyte is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by them.</small>

```

# Settings and themes

## Settings

**Settings → General …** holds the settings, stored in Grembyte's database. The list on the left chooses a page: General, Scan, Pointer scan, Trace, Hooks, Object browser and Wine/Proton.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Settings](../assets/screenshots/settings-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="640" }
  ![Settings](../assets/screenshots/settings-light.webp#only-light){ width="640" }
</figure>

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Language | Deutsch, English, or as the system (the default). Takes effect at the next start. |
| Refresh remembered addresses every (ms) | How often tracked addresses read their values (default 1000, 100 to 10 000). |
| Record the activity log | Write the [activity log](tools.md#log-and-activity) (off by default). Takes effect at once. |
| Aligned addresses only | The first [value scan](scanning.md#data-types) checks only addresses that are a multiple of the type's size (on by default). Faster and uses far less memory. |
| Pointer scan: Max. results | How many chains a [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md#search-limits) keeps (default 10 000, 100 to 1 million). More results take more memory, also in the database. |
| Pointer scan: Search thread stacks | Let chains pass through the thread stacks (off by default); see [memory regions](pointer-scan.md#memory-regions). |
| Pointer scan: Pointers lie at / Pointers point to | What counts as a pointer; both default to the pointer size of the program. See [alignment](pointer-scan.md#alignment). |
| Trace under Wine/Proton: at most methods | Most methods a trace hooks in a Wine/Proton game (default 5000, or no limit). Traces of tens of thousands of methods froze or crashed games there. |
| Trace: ask first from methods | From this many methods the trace asks before it starts; Mono has to compile them all (default 5000). |
| Trace: entries in the sequence | How many calls the trace and the native trace keep in order during the scenario (default 100 000, up to 500 000); raise it when the window reports dropped ones. |
| Automatically download the Wine/Proton Frida gadget | Off by default; see [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md). |
| Hooks: short jump in tight spots (experimental) | Off by default; see the [hook limitations](hooks.md#limitations). |
| Hooks: patch hooks the game removed again | Off by default. For games that check and restore their code, e.g. Dark Souls III. Grembyte checks every second and patches again. Can be detected by anti-tamper systems. |
| Hooks: measure their cost | Off by default. Measures every write at a hooked site: calls per second, skipped writes, waiting time and run time. Shown in the tooltip of the "Applied" column and in `grembyte.log`. |
| Object browser: objects read (Unity Mono) | How many live objects the [object browser](object-browser.md#unity-mono) keeps per read (default 2 million, up to 10 million). Each takes 16 bytes in the game while Grembyte is attached. Raise it when the browser reports that not all objects could be kept. Takes effect at the next refresh. |

**Defaults** fills in the default values on every page; **Save** stores them.

**Settings → Backend (watch & hooks)** chooses between Frida and ptrace; see [backends](write-watch.md#backends-frida-or-ptrace).

## Color themes

**Settings → Color theme …** chooses a theme or edits its colors. Changes preview immediately; **Save** stores the palette and activates it, **Cancel** discards the preview. Enter a new name in the theme selector to create a theme of your own.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Theme editor](../assets/screenshots/theme-editor-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Theme editor](../assets/screenshots/theme-editor-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

The bundled themes are **Github-Dark** (the default), **Github-Light**, **Solarized-Dark** and **Solarized-Light**. Themes of your own are saved as `grembyte_themes_<name>.json`; [Files and environment](../reference/files.md) says where.

## Window layout

Every window keeps its size, its splitters and the column widths you set; windows that are not modal also keep their position.

`docs/guide/templates.md`:

```md
# Hook templates

A manipulation is a JavaScript function that runs in the game after every hooked write. It receives a `ctx` object and returns the value to store; `undefined` or `null` keeps the game's value. Integer results are truncated and limited to the range of the type.

```js title="The built-in Multiplier"
function (ctx) {
  const { factor, direction } = ctx.params;
  if (direction === 'increase' && ctx.delta <= 0)
    return undefined;
  if (direction === 'decrease' && ctx.delta >= 0)
    return undefined;
  return ctx.old + ctx.delta * factor;
}
```

The fields of `ctx` are listed in the [hook context reference](../reference/hook-context.md).

## Managing templates

Manipulations are stored in the database as **hook templates** and managed under **View → Hook templates …**. At first start Grembyte creates the examples **Multiplier**, **Fixed value** and **Clamp** for value hooks and **Result × factor** and **Method script** for [method hooks](../engines/index.md); they can be changed or deleted like templates of your own. Their texts are English whatever the language of the interface, since templates are data that exports share.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hook templates](../assets/screenshots/hook-templates-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Hook templates](../assets/screenshots/hook-templates-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The built-in Multiplier with its parameters and its function.</figcaption>
</figure>

A template consists of a name, an optional description, its **Kind**, the JavaScript function and parameters. The kind says what the template is for: a **Value hook** changes a written value (`ctx.old`, `ctx.new`), a **Method hook** the arguments or the result of a method (`ctx.args`, `ctx.result`, see [method hooks](../reference/hook-context.md#method-hooks)). The hook dialogs offer only templates of their kind. Each parameter has

- a **name** – `ctx.params.<name>` in the script,
- a **label** shown in the hook dialog,
- a **type**: *Number*, *Choice* or *Code* for multi-line text,
- a **default**, and whether it is **optional**.

Choice values are written as `value=Label; value=Label`. The hook dialog builds its form from the parameters. A template with the number parameter `threshold` that only lets large gains through:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta >= ctx.params.threshold ? ctx.new : ctx.old
```

## Testing without a game

**Test** runs the function without a game process: enter the value type, the old value (`ctx.old`) and the value written by the game (`ctx.new`) and run it. It shows the stored value, the output of `ctx.log`/`console.log`, and errors. `ctx.state` is kept between test runs until **Reset state** clears it.

A method template is tested with a **Result of the method** instead. Without the game there are no arguments and objects: `ctx.args` and `ctx.refs` are empty, `ctx.this` and `ctx.caller` are `null`, and `ctx.call()` throws.

!!! note
    The test runs in Qt's JavaScript engine rather than in Frida, so Frida APIs such as `ptr()` or `Memory` are not available there.

## Templates and existing hooks

A hook stores a **copy** of the template it was created from, so later changes to the template do not affect existing hooks. In the hook's **Edit** dialog Grembyte points out a changed template and offers **Use changed template**. If the template is deleted, the hook keeps working with its copy.

## Examples

```js title="Never lose gold"
ctx => Math.max(ctx.new, ctx.old)
```

```js title="Count the calls and log every tenth"
ctx => {
  ctx.state.calls = (ctx.state.calls || 0) + 1;
  if (ctx.state.calls % 10 === 0) ctx.log(`call ${ctx.state.calls}: ${ctx.old} → ${ctx.new}`);
  return ctx.new;
}
```

```js title="Halve damage taken, keep healing as it is"
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```

# Docking, memory, sessions, logs and help

## Docking windows

Windows of their own cannot be kept beside the main window on every desktop (Wayland does not let programs place their windows). The tools you keep using while the game runs can therefore be docked in the main window instead: **Pin to main window** in the tool's window docks it as a tab, **Detach** gives it a window of its own again.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Docked tools](../assets/screenshots/main-window-docked-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Docked tools](../assets/screenshots/main-window-docked-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The memory viewer and an object inspector docked beside the scanner.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **At the side:** pointer scan, object inspector, object browser, write watch, memory viewer, GAS attributes, [notes](notes.md).
- **At the bottom**, where wide tables have room: trace, native trace, method monitor, native function monitor, log.
- Each side holds its windows as tabs. The ✕ on a tab, or a middle click, closes the window. A docked object inspector shows the object's name in its tab (else its class); the full title is in the tooltip.
- Grembyte remembers per kind of window whether the last one was docked: the next opens the same way. An object opened from a docked inspector opens as a tab beside it.
- When the game ends or another program is chosen, the tools close, docked or not. The log and the [notes](notes.md) stay, and so does the [pointer scan](pointer-scan.md#finding-a-chain): it is meant to find the value again after a restart.


## Memory viewer

**Memory** in the toolbar, or **Show in memory viewer** in the context menu of an address, shows the memory around an address as bytes and as text. It can be [docked](#docking-windows) beside the scanner.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Memory viewer](../assets/screenshots/memory-viewer-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Memory viewer](../assets/screenshots/memory-viewer-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The memory around the gold of the test game: 1350 is <code>46 05 00 00</code> in little-endian.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Sessions

**Sessions** in the toolbar lists Grembyte's connections to processes – Frida sessions and ptrace attachments – with what uses them. A session that no longer responds can be cut there:

- **Stop** lets the session remove its hooks and detach cleanly.
- **Disconnect** cuts the Frida session if it does not react to Stop. The part of Grembyte it belongs to (e.g. the hooks) then has to be started again.
- **Stop all** stops every session at once.

The **Sessions** button names how many there are; it warns when one does not respond to being stopped. Below the list the window says how many Frida agents the process has loaded. Agents left over from Grembyte runs that did not end cleanly cannot be removed from outside; only restarting the game clears them.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Sessions](../assets/screenshots/sessions-dark.webp#only-dark){ width="720" }
  ![Sessions](../assets/screenshots/sessions-light.webp#only-light){ width="720" }
</figure>

## Log and activity

**Log** in the status bar opens the log window. It turns red when errors were logged. The log can be [docked](#docking-windows) at the bottom of the main window; while its tab is in front, clicking **Log** again closes it.

The **Log** tab shows `grembyte.log`: what went wrong. **Warnings and errors only** hides the rest, **Copy** copies what is shown, and **Open folder** opens the folder with the log and `crash.log`, where Python's stack traces of crashes end up (see [files](../reference/files.md)).

The **Activity** tab shows the activity log: the course of every run, written to `activity.jsonl` in the log folder. It records

- the attached process with its details: 32 or 64 bit, native or Wine/Proton with the Proton version, engine, how the gadget was loaded;
- sessions and agents in the order they started and ended;
- every call into the game with its duration and outcome (frequent ones summed up);
- clicks in Grembyte, and why a Frida session ended, with Frida's crash report.

Values from the game's memory are not in it. The activity log is off by default: switch it on under **Settings → General …** (**Record the activity log**), best before you reproduce a problem.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Activity log](../assets/screenshots/log-activity-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Activity log](../assets/screenshots/log-activity-light.webp#only-light)
</figure>

**Export bug report …** packs the activity, the log and `crash.log` into a ZIP file – the best thing to attach to a bug report.

## Help menu

- **Documentation** opens this documentation in the browser.
- **Report a bug …** opens the bug report form on GitHub. Attach the ZIP from **Export bug report …**.
- **About Grembyte …** shows the version and the components Grembyte is built on, with their licenses.

`docs/guide/write-watch.md`:

```md
# Write and read watch

The address watch answers the question *which code changes this value?* It sets a hardware watchpoint on the address: the processor stops the game for a moment after every write (or every access), and Grembyte records the instruction responsible.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Write watch](../assets/screenshots/write-watch-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The increase and the decrease of the gold each show up as a row of their own; a third location only reads it.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Starting a watch

Right-click a tracked address or a scan result:

- **Address watch (writes)** reports every instruction that writes the address.
- **Address watch (all accesses)** also reports instructions that read it. x86 watchpoints trap on writes or on any access, there is no read-only mode; Grembyte decodes each instruction to tell whether it reads, writes or both.

Then do in the game what changes the value. Each code location gets one row, with how often it hit and the bytes it left at the address. The columns **Reads** and **Writes** show what the row's instruction does with the value. In Mono games a hit in JIT code also names its C# method; in IL2CPP games code in `GameAssembly` is named as the C# method it belongs to.

Select a writing row and click **Create hook …** to [hook](hooks.md) it. Hooks can only be set on writing instructions. **Monitor location** hands the row's code location to the [native function monitor](native-tools.md#native-function-monitor): the registers at every pass, and if wanted the function it lies in. **Stop monitoring** ends the watch.

The watch can be [docked](tools.md#docking-windows) beside the scanner, so it stays in view while you play.

Hooks and [scripts](scripts.md) keep working while a watch is set: a game method a script calls, or a value it reads or writes itself (`ptr.writeS32(…)`), runs to its end, and the watch lists the access like any other.

## Backends: Frida or ptrace

The watch (and hooks) run through **Frida (injection)** by default. **Settings → Backend (watch & hooks)** switches to **ptrace (debugger)**, which needs no injection into the game:

| | Frida | ptrace (Linux only) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Injection into the game | yes | no |
| Addresses at once | several | at most 4 (debug registers) |
| Hook training and caller learning | yes | no |
| 32-bit Wine/Proton games | – | chosen automatically |

The status bar shows the backend in use.

With `ptrace`, a watchpoint can cover 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes only when its address is aligned to that size. Grembyte rejects an unaligned address instead of setting the watchpoint.

!!! warning "Anti-tamper and debug registers"
    Some anti-tamper protections detect the debug registers that watchpoints use; Dark Souls III crashed. Grembyte points it out when a game ends shortly after debug registers were used.

```

```md
# Grembyte

Grembyte is a desktop application for inspecting and changing the memory of running games. It finds values such as gold or health, shows which code writes them, and hooks that code so every write is changed the way you want: a multiplier, a fixed value, bounds, or a JavaScript function of your own. Hooks, addresses and scripts are stored per game and come back the next time it starts.

It runs on **Linux**, including Windows games under **[Wine and Proton](wine-proton.md)**, and on **Windows**. For Unity (Mono and IL2CPP) and Unreal Engine games it also understands the game's own classes and methods.

!!! info "Alpha stage"
    Grembyte is still in an early alpha stage. Features, the user interface and the format of saved game data can still change between releases, and some games or setups may not work yet. Bug reports and game reports are welcome on [GitHub](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/issues).

markdown="span">
  ![Grembyte main window with scan results and tracked addresses](assets/screenshots/main-window-dark.webp#only-dark)
  ![Grembyte main window with scan results and tracked addresses](assets/screenshots/main-window-light.webp#only-light)
  <figcaption>The main window after a few scans for the gold of the test game: results on the left, the value search on the right, tracked addresses with their pointer chains below.</figcaption>
</figure>

!!! warning "Single-player only"
    This tool is intended solely for educational, research and single-player game modding purposes. It is not designed or intended to bypass anti-cheat mechanisms or to be used in online multiplayer games. The developer assumes no responsibility or liability for any account bans, suspensions or damages resulting from the use or misuse of this software.

    Restoring memory modifications that a game removed can be detected by anti-tamper systems (such as Arxan) and, when used online, carries a considerable risk of account bans or soft bans. Use it at your own risk.

## What it does

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-magnify:{ .lg .middle } **Find values**

    ---

    Scan for integers and floats: exact, ranges, unknown initial value, changed or increased by an amount, with tolerance and rounded floats.

-   :material-link-variant:{ .lg .middle } **Keep them across restarts**

    [:octicons-arrow-right-24: Object browser](guide/object-browser.md)

-   :material-chart-timeline-variant:{ .lg .middle } **Trace native functions**

    ---

    For games without an engine Grembyte knows: which functions a scenario calls, and what one of them gets, returns and changes.

-   :material-file-search-outline:{ .lg .middle } **Explore native code**

## Where to start

1. [Download and install](getting-started/installation.md) Grembyte (no GitHub experience needed) and check the [permissions](getting-started/permissions.md) it needs on Linux.
2. Follow the [tutorial](getting-started/first-hook.md): with the small test game in the repository you find a value, watch its writes and hook them, in about ten minutes.
3. Read the [user guide](guide/scanning.md) for the details of each tool, and the [engine pages](engines/index.md) for Unity and Unreal games.
4. Try everything on [HermesQuest](examples/index.md), a small Unity role-playing game made for it, with worked examples of pointer scans, hooks and scripts – and an introduction to [JavaScript in Grembyte](reference/javascript.md). Examples for native games use the test game of the tutorial.

!!! info "Under development"
    Grembyte is under active development. The [roadmap](https://github.com/grembyte/grembyte/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) lists what is planned and what is still open.

```md
# Assembly (x86-64)

The [code explorer](../guide/code-explorer.md), the [write watch](../guide/write-watch.md) and the [native tools](../guide/native-tools.md) show machine code as assembly: one line per instruction. You do not need to write assembly to use Grembyte, but reading a few lines tells you what a function does, which arguments it takes and which value it changes. This page covers what that takes, for the x86-64 code of today's games; the [code explorer example](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md) applies it step by step.

## Reading a line

```text
0x4006d7  48 8b 40 28   mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]
address   bytes         mnemonic  operands
```

- **Address:** where the instruction is. The code explorer shows addresses of the file; in the running game the module may sit elsewhere (`module+0x6d7` stays the same).
- **Bytes:** the machine code itself. Byte patterns for scripts are made of these, with `??` for the parts that change between builds.
- **Mnemonic:** what the instruction does, here `mov` (copy).
- **Operands:** what it works on. Grembyte shows Intel syntax, the **destination comes first**: `mov rax, [rax + 0x28]` means *rax = the 8 bytes at address rax + 0x28*.

Numbers are hexadecimal when they start with `0x`. A negative displacement reads `[rbp - 0x10]`.

## Registers

The processor's own variables. Each 64-bit register has smaller parts with names of their own; writing a 32-bit part clears the upper half, writing an 8- or 16-bit part leaves the rest alone.

| 64 bits | 32 bits | 16 bits | 8 bits | Usual role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rax` | `eax` | `ax` | `al` | result of a function |
| `rbx` | `ebx` | `bx` | `bl` | kept across calls |
| `rcx` | `ecx` | `cx` | `cl` | 4th argument (Linux), 1st (Windows); shift count |
| `rdx` | `edx` | `dx` | `dl` | 3rd argument (Linux), 2nd (Windows) |
| `rsi` | `esi` | `si` | `sil` | 2nd argument (Linux) |
| `rdi` | `edi` | `di` | `dil` | 1st argument (Linux) |
| `rbp` | `ebp` | `bp` | `bpl` | frame pointer, or kept across calls |
| `rsp` | `esp` | `sp` | `spl` | stack pointer: the top of the stack |
| `r8`–`r15` | `r8d`–`r15d` | `r8w`–`r15w` | `r8b`–`r15b` | more arguments (`r8`, `r9`), scratch, kept across calls (`r12`–`r15`) |

Others you meet:

- **`rip`**, the instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction. `[rip + 0x2a31]` is an address relative to the code, the usual way to reach a **global variable** or a string; the code explorer shows the result (`g_game`).
- **`xmm0`–`xmm15`**: 128-bit registers for floating point (and SIMD). A `float` uses their lowest 4 bytes, a `double` 8. `ymm`/`zmm` are their 256- and 512-bit forms.
- **Flags** (`rflags`): bits set by comparisons and arithmetic (zero, sign, carry, overflow), read by conditional jumps.

The size of a value follows from the register name: `eax` is an `int`, `al` a `bool` or byte, `rax` a pointer or 64-bit number. In memory operands the size is spelled out: `byte ptr` (1), `word ptr` (2), `dword ptr` (4), `qword ptr` (8).

## Operands

| Form | Example | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register | `rax` | the register's value |
| Immediate | `0x14` | a constant in the instruction |
| Memory | `[rax]` | the value at the address in `rax` |
| Base + displacement | `[rax + 0x28]` | a field of a struct or object `rax` points to |
| Base + index × scale | `[rax + rcx*4]` | element `rcx` of an array of 4-byte values |
| RIP-relative | `[rip + 0x2a31]` | a global variable or constant near the code |

`lea` computes the address of a memory operand **without reading memory**: `lea rax, [rdi + 8]` is *rax = rdi + 8*. Compilers also use it for plain arithmetic: `lea edx, [rdx + rdx*4]` is *edx = edx × 5*.

## Instructions

### Moving data

| Instruction | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `mov a, b` | a = b |
| `movzx a, b` | a = b, the smaller b zero-extended (unsigned) |
| `movsx` / `movsxd a, b` | a = b, sign-extended (signed) |
| `lea a, [address]` | a = the address itself (no memory access) |
| `push a` / `pop a` | put a on the stack / take the top of the stack into a |
| `xchg a, b` | swap |
| `cmovcc a, b` | a = b if the condition holds (`cmovl`, `cmove`, …: see the jumps) |
| `setcc a` | a (a byte) = 1 if the condition holds, else 0: a `bool` |

### Arithmetic and logic

| Instruction | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `add a, b` / `sub a, b` | a += b / a -= b |
| `inc a` / `dec a` | a += 1 / a -= 1 |
| `neg a` | a = -a |
| `imul a, b` / `imul a, b, c` | a *= b / a = b × c (signed) |
| `mul` / `div` / `idiv` | multiply / divide using `rdx:rax` (rare: compilers prefer the tricks below) |
| `and` / `or` / `xor a, b` | bitwise; `xor eax, eax` sets eax to 0 |
| `not a` | flip all bits |
| `shl` / `shr` / `sar a, n` | shift left (× 2ⁿ) / right unsigned / right signed (÷ 2ⁿ) |

### Comparing and branching

`cmp a, b` computes a − b and `test a, b` computes a AND b, both only for the flags; the jump after them decides.

| Jump | Taken if (after `cmp a, b`) | Signed? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `je` / `jz` | a == b (after `test a, a`: a == 0) | |
| `jne` / `jnz` | a != b | |
| `jl` / `jge` | a < b / a >= b | signed |
| `jle` / `jg` | a <= b / a > b | signed |
| `jb` / `jae` | a < b / a >= b | unsigned |
| `jbe` / `ja` | a <= b / a > b | unsigned |
| `js` / `jns` | the result is negative / not | |
| `jmp` | always | |

The same conditions name `cmovcc` and `setcc`: `setg al`, `cmovl eax, edx`. Whether a comparison uses signed or unsigned conditions tells you whether the value is signed.

### Calling

| Instruction | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `call f` | push the return address, jump to f |
| `call qword ptr [rax + 0x18]` | call through a pointer: a C++ virtual method, a callback, an imported function |
| `ret` | return to the address on the stack |
| `jmp f` at the end of a function | a *tail call*: f returns straight to our caller |

### Floating point (SSE)

The suffix tells the type: `ss` = one `float`, `sd` = one `double`, `ps`/`pd` = several at once.

| Instruction | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `movss` / `movsd` | copy a float / double |
| `addss`, `subss`, `mulss`, `divss` (and `…sd`) | arithmetic |
| `ucomiss` / `comiss` (and `…sd`) | compare, followed by a jump (`ja`, `jb`, … as for unsigned numbers) |
| `cvtsi2ss` / `cvttss2si` | int → float / float → int (truncated) |
| `cvtss2sd` / `cvtsd2ss` | float → double / double → float |
| `xorps xmm0, xmm0` | xmm0 = 0.0 |
| `sqrtss`, `minss`, `maxss` | square root, minimum, maximum |

### Seen often, doing little

`nop` (nothing, padding), `int3` (breakpoint, padding between functions), `endbr64` (marks a valid jump target), `leave` (undo the stack frame before `ret`).

## Patterns that come up again and again

| Code | Reads as |
| --- | --- |
| `xor eax, eax` | `eax = 0` |
| `test eax, eax` / `je L` | `if (eax == 0) goto L` |
| `cmp ecx, 0x63` / `jg L` | `if (ecx > 99) goto L` (signed) |
| `mov rax, [rip + x]` / `mov rax, [rax + 0x28]` | `rax = global->field` (a pointer chain) |
| `add dword ptr [rax], edi` | `*rax += edi` (a 4-byte value changed: what a write watch reports) |
| `mov eax, [rcx + rdx*4]` | `eax = array[rdx]` (4-byte elements) |
| `mov rax, [rcx]` / `call qword ptr [rax + 0x30]` | `rcx->virtualMethod()`: the object's vtable, its 7th entry (0x30 / 8 = 6, counted from 0) |
| `movzx eax, byte ptr [rdi + 0x174]` / `test al, al` | read a `bool` field |
| `setne al` / `movzx eax, al` / `ret` | `return x != y;` |
| `push rbx` … `sub rsp, 0x20` … `add rsp, 0x20` / `pop rbx` / `ret` | prologue and epilogue: saving registers and room on the stack, not game logic |
| `mov eax, 0x2f80` / `call __chkstk` / `sub rsp, rax` | a large stack frame (Windows) |
| `mov rax, [rip + __security_cookie]` / `xor rax, rsp` | a stack protector, not game logic |
| `imul rdx, rdx, 0x2e8ba2e9` / `sar rdx, 0x21` | division by a constant (here 11): compilers multiply by a "magic" number instead of dividing |
| `lea eax, [rax + rax*2]` / `shl eax, 2` | `eax × 3`, then `× 4`: multiplication without `imul` |

## Reading a function: add_gold

From the test game of the [tutorial](../getting-started/first-hook.md):

```text
mov rax, qword ptr [rip + 0x2a31]   ; rax = g_game           (a global)
mov rax, qword ptr [rax + 0x28]     ; rax = g_game->player   (field at +0x28)
add dword ptr [rax], edi            ; player->gold += amount (first argument, an int)
ret                                 ; return, nothing in eax that callers use
```

In C: `void add_gold(int amount) { g_game->player->gold += amount; }`.

A longer one, `on_treasure`, with a division in disguise:

```text
call rand                         ; eax = rand()
movsxd rdx, eax                   ; rdx = eax (signed, 64-bit)
mov ecx, eax
imul rdx, rdx, 0x2e8ba2e9         ; ┐
sar ecx, 0x1f                     ; │ edx = eax / 11
sar rdx, 0x21                     ; │ (multiplied by a magic number,
sub edx, ecx                      ; ┘  corrected for negative numbers)
lea ecx, [rdx + rdx*4]            ; ecx = 5 × quotient
lea edx, [rdx + rcx*2]            ; edx = 11 × quotient
sub eax, edx                      ; eax = rand() - 11 × quotient = rand() % 11
lea edi, [rax + 0x14]             ; edi = that + 20          → the argument
call add_gold                     ; add_gold(20 + rand() % 11)
add rsp, 8
jmp refresh_ui                    ; tail call: refresh_ui(), then back to our caller
```

How to approach an unknown function:

1. **Read the comments first.** The code explorer names strings, functions, imports and globals; often they tell the story (`"Not enough gold"`, `SDL_PlaySound`).
2. **Look at the calls.** What a function calls says more than its arithmetic.
3. **Find the memory writes.** `mov [reg + offset], …`, `add [reg], …`: which fields of which object change.
4. **Follow the arguments** from their registers (see the calling conventions below) to where they are used.
5. **Skip prologue and epilogue**, stack protectors and `__chkstk`.

## Calling conventions

Where a function finds its arguments and leaves its result:

| | Linux (System V) | Windows and Wine/Proton |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integer and pointer arguments | `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`, then the stack | `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, then the stack |
| `float` and `double` arguments | `xmm0`–`xmm7` | `xmm0`–`xmm3`, at the argument's position |
| Result | `rax`, or `xmm0` | `rax`, or `xmm0` |
| A call may change | `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `rsi`, `rdi`, `r8`–`r11`, `xmm0`–`xmm15` | `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`–`r11`, `xmm0`–`xmm5` |
| A call keeps | `rbx`, `rbp`, `r12`–`r15` | `rbx`, `rbp`, `rdi`, `rsi`, `r12`–`r15`, `xmm6`–`xmm15` |
| C++ `this` | the first argument | the first argument |

That is why a value a function needs after a call sits in `rbx` or `r12`–`r15`, and why the first instructions often copy argument registers there. How to tell a function's arguments and result from its code is on the example page: [What add_gold takes](../examples/dummy-game-code-explorer.md#4-what-add_gold-takes).

## 32-bit code

32-bit programs use `eax`, `ebx`, `ecx`, `edx`, `esi`, `edi`, `ebp`, `esp` (no `r8`–`r15`, no `rip`-relative addressing). Arguments are usually pushed on the stack (`push`, then `call`) and read as `[esp + 4]`, `[ebp + 8]`; globals appear as absolute addresses (`mov eax, [0x5a4f10]`). C++ methods compiled with MSVC pass `this` in `ecx`.

## Further reading

- [Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual](https://intel.github.io/SDM/sdm.html): Intel's own reference, with every instruction and its exact effect.
- [Compiler Explorer](https://godbolt.org/): type C or C++ and see the assembly a compiler makes of it; the best way to learn what code looks like.

# Files and environment

## Where Grembyte keeps its data

| What | Linux | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Database (`grembyte.db`) | `~/.local/share/grembyte/` (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/grembyte/`) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\grembyte\` |
| Catalog cache | `~/.local/share/grembyte/cache/` (`$GREMBYTE_CACHE_DIR`) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\grembyte\cache\` |
| Wine/Proton gadgets | `~/.local/share/grembyte/gadget/` | – |
| Logs (`grembyte.log`, `crash.log`, `activity.jsonl`) | `~/.local/state/grembyte/` (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/grembyte/`) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\grembyte\logs\` |
| Themes of your own | `~/.config/grembyte/themes/` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/grembyte/themes/`) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\grembyte\themes\` |
| Link between the window and [grembyte-cli](../guide/launch-option.md) (`cli-<pid>.json`, `cli-<pid>.sock`) | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/grembyte/` (else `grembyte-<user>/` in the temp folder) | – |
| Window sizes and UI state | Qt settings `grembyte/grembyte` | Qt settings (registry) |

Bundled themes ship in `grembyte/ui/themes/`, as `grembyte_themes_<name>.json` like your own.

If there is no database yet but one from earlier versions at `data/hermes.db` in the project directory, Grembyte copies it once; the original stays.

### Files from Hermes Hook

Up to version 0.6 Grembyte was called Hermes Hook and kept its files in folders named `hermes-hook`. On its first start Grembyte moves these folders to `grembyte`, renames `hermes.db`, `hermes.log` and your themes (`hermes_themes_*.json` to `grembyte_themes_*.json`) and copies the window sizes from the old Qt settings. A file that already exists under the new name is kept. The log lists what was taken over.

The environment variables changed their names too: set `GREMBYTE_DB` instead of `HERMES_DB`, and so on. A menu entry or Start menu shortcut installed for Hermes Hook is replaced when you run the install script again (see [Installation](../getting-started/installation.md)).

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `GREMBYTE_DB` | Use another database file. |
| `GREMBYTE_CACHE_DIR` | Keep the catalog cache elsewhere. |
| `GREMBYTE_LOG_DIR` | Write logs and the activity log to another folder. |
| `GREMBYTE_LANGUAGE` | `de` or `en` for one start, while the language setting is "as the system". |
| `GREMBYTE_INJECT_DIR` | Folder with the Wine helper executables (see [Wine and Proton](../wine-proton.md)). |
| `GREMBYTE_VENV` | Virtual environment used by `scripts/grembyte.sh`. |

`docs/reference/hook-context.md`:

```md
# Hook context (`ctx`)

The object a [hook template](../guide/templates.md) and a method hook's script receive. The script returns the value to store; `undefined` or `null` keeps the game's value.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.old` | Value before the write |
| `ctx.new` | Value the game wrote |
| `ctx.delta` | `ctx.new - ctx.old` |
| `ctx.params` | The template's parameters with the hook's values, by name |
| `ctx.state` | Object kept between calls, e.g. for counters |
| `ctx.this` | Method hooks only: the instance the method runs on; `null` for static methods |
| `ctx.valueType` | The value type, e.g. `"int32"` or `"float"` |
| `ctx.address` | Address that was written |
| `ctx.writePc` | Address of the write instruction |
| `ctx.threadId` | Thread that wrote |
| `ctx.hookId` | Database id of the hook |
| `ctx.log(…)`, `console.log(…)` | Output in the hook log and the debug window |

Integer results are truncated and limited to the range of the type. `int64` and `uint64` values are exact only up to 2^53.

!!! note "Hooks of the ptrace backend"
    With the `ptrace` [backend](../guide/hooks.md) the script runs in Grembyte, not in the game, after the game wrote the value. The fields are as above, each hook with its own `ctx.state`, and `ctx.log` writes to the hook log; only `ctx.writePc` is `"0x0"`, since the watchpoint reports the instruction after the write. Frida's APIs (`ptr()`, `Memory`, …) are not available there.

## Method hooks

A method hook's script runs before or after the hooked method (**When**). Besides `ctx.params`, `ctx.state`, `ctx.this`, `ctx.log(…)` and `ctx.hookId` it gets:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ctx.phase` | `"before"` or `"after"` the call |
| `ctx.args.<name>` | The method's arguments by name. Before the call, assigning one (`ctx.args.amount = 0`) changes what the method gets. |
| `ctx.result` | After the call: the method's result (`undefined` for `void` methods). A returned value replaces it. |
| `ctx.refs.<name>` | After the call: what `ref` and `out` arguments hold |
| `ctx.caller` | The innermost hooked call this call runs in, if that hook runs "after the call": an object with `.method`, `.this`, `.args` and `.caller`; otherwise `null` |
| `ctx.method` | The hooked method |
| `ctx.threadId` | Thread the call runs on |
| `ctx.call(method, ...args)` | Call a static game method, as in [scripts](script-context.md) |
| `ctx.static(field)` | Mono and IL2CPP: read a static field |
| `ctx.find(className[, objectName])`, `ctx.forEach(…)`, `ctx.outerName(…)` | Find live objects, as in [scripts](script-context.md) |

Objects – `ctx.this`, object arguments, results – are the same [wrappers as in scripts](script-context.md#object-wrappers): fields, properties and methods directly (`target.IsPlayer`, `obj.GetComponentByName("Stats")`). Before the call, assigning a field (`obj.Field = …`) or property (which calls its setter) changes what the method works with.

In Unreal games a hook called from Blueprint bytecode only gets arguments that are simple variables or constants, and only `ref` arguments can be changed. See [Engines](../engines/index.md#method-hooks) for an overview and the [HermesQuest examples](../examples/hermesquest-hooks.md#method-hooks) for method hooks step by step.

The [Scripts](../guide/scripts.md) tab has a `ctx` of its own, described in the [script context reference](script-context.md).

```

`docs/reference/javascript.md`:

```md
# JavaScript in Grembyte

Grembyte uses JavaScript wherever you tell it *what* to do with a value or with the game: hook templates, method hooks and scripts. You need little of the language for that. This page explains that part, along the [HermesQuest](../examples/index.md) examples – no previous knowledge of JavaScript assumed.

## Where JavaScript is used

| Where | Shape | Runs | Gets | Its `return` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Hook template](../guide/templates.md) (value hook) | a **function**: `ctx => …` or `function (ctx) { … }` | after every hooked write, in the writing thread | `ctx.old`, `ctx.new`, `ctx.delta`, `ctx.params`, `ctx.state` | the value to store; nothing keeps the game's value |
| [Method hook](../examples/hermesquest-hooks.md#method-hooks) with *Method script* | the **body** of a function: just the statements | before or after every call of the method | `ctx.args`, `ctx.this`, `ctx.result`, `ctx.phase`, `ctx.call`, `ctx.static`, `ctx.find` | after the call: the new result |
| [Script](../examples/hermesquest-scripts.md) | the **body** of a function | by hand or on a timer, on the game's main thread | `ctx.static`, `ctx.find`, `ctx.call`, `ctx.args`, `ctx.state`, `ctx.log` | shown as the script's result |
| Options of a choice parameter | the **body** of a function | when the run dialog asks for them | the same `ctx` as scripts | the list of options |

All of them get one object, `ctx` (for *context*), through which they reach everything else. The [hook context](hook-context.md) and [script context](script-context.md) references list its fields.

A **function** is code with a name for its input; a **body** is just the code inside. A template is a function because Grembyte stores and tests it on its own; a script is a body because Grembyte wraps it into a function for you:

```js
// A function (hook template): input ctx, result after =>
ctx => ctx.new * 2

// A body (script): statements, ctx is simply there
const stats = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player.Stats;
return stats.Gold;
```

## Statements, comments and names

A script is a list of **statements**, run from top to bottom. A statement usually ends with `;` – JavaScript tolerates missing ones, but writing them avoids surprises.

```js
// A comment: from // to the end of the line, ignored.
/* A longer comment
   over several lines. */

const player = ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current").Player;
let healed = 0;
healed = player.Heal(5);
```

- `const name = value;` gives a value a name. It cannot be given another value later – use it by default.
- `let name = value;` is the same, but may change later (`healed = …`).
- Names are **case-sensitive**: `player` and `Player` are different, and so are the game's fields – `Stats.Health`, never `stats.health`.

## Values

### Numbers

JavaScript has one number type: a 64-bit floating-point number (C#'s `double`). Grembyte converts the game's types for you:

| Game type | In JavaScript | Watch out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int`, `short`, `byte` … | number | When writing one back, cut decimals off with `Math.trunc` or `Math.round`. In value hooks Grembyte truncates integer results itself. |
| `long` (`int64`) | number | Exact only up to 2^53 (about 9 × 10^15). |
| `float` | number | The game keeps only about 7 significant digits. |
| `double` | number | Same precision as JavaScript. |

Calculating works as expected: `+ - * /`, `%` for the remainder, parentheses for order. Useful functions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `Math.round(x)`, `Math.trunc(x)`, `Math.floor(x)`, `Math.ceil(x)` | round, cut off, round down, round up |
| `Math.min(a, b)`, `Math.max(a, b)` | the smaller, the larger value |
| `Math.abs(x)` | the value without its sign |
| `x.toFixed(2)` | `x` as text with two decimal places, for display |

!!! warning "Comparing floats"
    `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` is `false` in JavaScript, as in almost every language: most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly. A `float` from the game, read into JavaScript's `double`, is a little off as well. Compare with a tolerance instead:

    ```js
    if (Math.abs(stats.Mana - 42.5) < 0.001) …
    ```

### Text

Text (a *string*) is written in quotes: `"Hero"` or `'Hero'`. For text with values in it, use backticks and `${…}`:

```js
ctx.log(`${enemy.Name} has ${enemy.Stats.Health.toFixed(1)} health`);
// Goblin has 7.5 health
```

To test, take apart or clean up texts – names with a running number, numbers in a label – use [regular expressions](regex.md): `obj.name.replace(/_\d+$/, "")`.

### True and false

Comparisons give `true` or `false`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `a === b`, `a !== b` | equal, not equal |
| `a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b`, `a >= b` | smaller, greater … |
| `x && y` | `x` **and** `y` |
| `x || y` | `x` **or** `y` |
| `!x` | **not** `x` |

Always use `===` and `!==`. The shorter `==` converts values before comparing (`"1" == 1` is `true`), which hides mistakes.

### Nothing: `null` and `undefined`

- `null` means *no object*: `game.NearestEnemy(player, 8)` gives `null` when no enemy is near, `ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current")` before the first game exists.
- `undefined` means *not set*: a field of `ctx.state` you have not stored yet, or a function that ends without `return`.

Using a field of `null` is an error (`cannot read property 'Stats' of null`), so check first:

```js
const enemy = game.NearestEnemy(player, 8);
if (enemy === null)
  return "No enemy near";
ctx.log(enemy.Name);
```

## Decisions: `if`

```js
if (ctx.args.attacker.IsPlayer) {
  return ctx.result * 3;
} else if (ctx.args.target.IsPlayer) {
  return ctx.result / 2;
} else {
  ctx.log("enemy against enemy");
}
```

The block in `{ … }` runs only if the condition in `( … )` is `true`. With a single statement the braces may be left out, as in the [hooks examples](../examples/hermesquest-hooks.md#only-the-player-hits-harder-and-takes-less).

`return` ends the script (or function) at once. Everything after it is skipped – that is how `if (game === null) return;` stops a script early.

## Arrow functions and the conditional operator

Hook templates are usually one line:

```js
ctx => ctx.delta < 0 ? ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2 : ctx.new
```

Two pieces of syntax do the work:

- `ctx => …` is an **arrow function**: it takes `ctx` and gives back what follows the arrow.
- `condition ? a : b` is the **conditional operator**: `a` if the condition is true, else `b`.

So the template reads: *take `ctx`; if the value went down, give back the old value plus half the change, otherwise the value the game wrote.* With the player at 40 health and a hit of 6 the game writes 34; `ctx.delta` is −6, and the hook stores 40 + (−6 / 2) = 37.

The same in the long form, which can hold several statements:

```js
function (ctx) {
  if (ctx.delta < 0)
    return ctx.old + ctx.delta / 2;
  return ctx.new;
}
```

Both forms are fine for templates. Returning nothing (`undefined`) or `null` keeps what the game wrote.

## Lists and objects

A **list** (array) holds values in order, in square brackets; an **object** holds named values, in braces:

```js
const names = ["Strength", "Dexterity", "Intelligence"];
names[0]          // "Strength" – counting starts at 0
names.length      // 3

const option = { label: "Strength (melee damage)", value: "Strength" };
option.label      // "Strength (melee damage)"
```

Going through all entries of a list:

```js
for (const name of names)
  ctx.log(`${name}: ${stats[name]}`);
```

`stats[name]` reads the field whose name is in the variable `name` – the same as `stats.Strength` when `name` is `"Strength"`.

`ctx.state` is such an object. Store what a hook or script should remember in it:

```js
ctx.state.calls = (ctx.state.calls || 0) + 1;
```

`(ctx.state.calls || 0)` is the stored count, or 0 the first time, when it is still `undefined`.

## Game objects

What `ctx.static`, `ctx.find`, `ctx.args`, `ctx.this` or a method give you for an object of the game is a **wrapper**: a JavaScript object that reads from and writes to the game's memory each time you use it.

| You write | Grembyte does |
| --- | --- |
| `player.Stats` | reads the field `Stats` – an object again |
| `stats.Health` | reads the field `Health` from the game's memory, now |
| `stats.Health = 50` | writes 50 into the field |
| `player.IsDead` | runs the property's getter `get_IsDead` in the game |
| `player.Heal(10)` | calls the method `Heal` with 10 and gives its result |
| `ctx.call("HermesQuest.Combat:HitChance", player, enemy)` | calls a static method; objects can be passed along |
| `ctx.static("HermesQuest.GameState.Current")` | reads a static field |
| `player.className` | the object's class, `"HermesQuest.Character"` |

Because every read goes to the game, a value read twice may differ – mana regenerates between the two reads. Read it once into a `const` if you need it several times.

The wrapper's own names come first: `name`, `className`, `address`, `field`, `get`, `call`, and in Unity `component`. If the game has a field of one of these names, read it with `obj.field("name")`. All that a wrapper offers is listed in the [script context reference](script-context.md#object-wrappers).

!!! tip "Finding the names"
    Return an object from a script, or click an object in the method monitor: the **object inspector** lists its fields, properties and methods with their exact names and types. The [catalog](../engines/index.md#catalog) lists every class and method.

## Finding mistakes

- **`ctx.log(…)`** writes to the script log; in hooks to the hook log below the Hooks tab and to the debug window. Log values to see what the code works with: `ctx.log(ctx.old, ctx.new, ctx.delta)`.
- **Test** in the template editor runs a value template without the game: enter old and new value and see what it stores. It runs in Qt's JavaScript engine, so Frida's functions (`ptr`, `Memory`) are missing there.
- **Debug** in the Hooks tab logs every call of the selected hooks with old value, game value, result, log output and errors.
- **Errors** appear with their message in the log. A value hook whose script fails keeps the game's value; a script that fails stops this run only.

## Things to remember

- Scripts and method hooks run **inside the game**, on its thread: keep them short. A loop that waits for something blocks the game.
- A value hook runs at **every write** of its instruction, possibly thousands of times a second. Avoid `ctx.log` there except while debugging.
- Writing a field bypasses the game's rules; calling its method follows them.
- After "New game" every object is new. Scripts that ask `ctx.static(…)` each run find the new ones by themselves.

```md
# Markdown

Markdown is plain text with a few characters that format it: `## Gold` becomes a heading, `- ` a list item, `` `AddGold` `` code. The [notes](../guide/notes.md) are written in Markdown; their **Preview** tab shows the text formatted. This page covers the commands the preview understands. They are those of GitHub (the same text looks almost the same in a GitHub issue or README), with a few differences listed under [What the preview does not show](#what-the-preview-does-not-show).

## Text

| Write | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `**bold**` | **bold** |
| `*italic*` | *italic* |
| `***bold and italic***` | ***bold and italic*** |
| `~~struck through~~` | <del>struck through</del> |
| `` `AddGold(int)` `` | `AddGold(int)` – code, in a fixed-width font, nothing inside is formatted |
| ``` `` a `tick` inside `` ``` | `` a `tick` inside `` – two backticks around code that holds one |
| `_underlined_` | underlined in Grembyte, *italic* on GitHub – use `*…*` for italic |

Underscores inside a word do nothing: `Player_Gold_Amount` stays as it is.

## Headings

```markdown
# Game
## Gold
### Where it is written
```

`#` to `######` give six levels; a space follows the `#`. In notes, `##` per topic (gold, experience, items) and `###` below it keep them easy to scan.

## Paragraphs and lines

- An empty line starts a new paragraph.
- A single line break is not kept: the lines run on as one paragraph. That way long sentences may be wrapped in the editor.
- Two spaces or a backslash `\` at the end of a line start a new line. Grembyte's preview shows it with the spacing of a new paragraph.

## Lists

```markdown
- Gold
- Experience
  - from quests
  - from enemies
1. Open the inventory
2. Call `AddItem`
- [x] Gold found
- [ ] Find the stamina
```

| Write | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `- `, `* ` or `+ ` at the start | a bulleted list |
| `1. ` or `1) ` | a numbered list (it counts on by itself, whatever the next numbers are) |
| indented to the text of the item above (two spaces under `- `, three under `1. `) | an item of that item's list |
| `- [ ] ` / `- [x] ` | a task with an empty / ticked check box |

The check boxes of the preview only show; tick a task by writing `x` between the brackets.

## Code

A word or name in backticks is code: `` `PlayerInventory:AddGold (int)` ``. Several lines go between lines of three backticks; a language may follow the first:

````markdown
```js
const gold = ctx.call("PlayerInventory:get_Gold");
ctx.log(`gold: ${gold}`);
```
````

The preview shows code in a fixed-width font, code blocks in a shaded box. The language decides the colors, in the preview and in the **Write** tab: `js`, `javascript`, `ts`, `typescript` and `json` are colored as JavaScript, `c`, `cpp` and `h` as C; code of other languages, or with none, is shown in one color. A paragraph indented by four spaces is code as well (in the preview; the Write tab does not color it).

!!! tip "Put names of the game in backticks"
    Names of classes, methods and fields often hold characters Markdown reads as commands: `List<Item>` looks like an HTML tag, `*` in `int*` or `_` at the start of `_gold` like emphasis. In backticks, everything stays as written.

## Links

| Write | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `[Wiki](https://example.com/wiki)` | a link named *Wiki* |
| `https://example.com` | the address as a link |
| `<https://example.com>` | the same |

Links open in your web browser.

## Tables

```markdown
| Value      | Offset | Type   |
| ---------- | -----: | ------ |
| Gold       |  `0x0` | int32  |
| Experience | `0x18` | double |
```

The second line separates the header from the rows. A colon sets how a column is aligned: `:---` left, `:---:` centered, `---:` right (useful for numbers). The columns need not line up in the text. A `|` inside a cell is written `\|`.

## Quotes and lines

| Write | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `> Text` | the text indented, as a quote |
| `---` on a line of its own (with empty lines around it) | a horizontal line |

An import that adds text to a note puts such a line between the old and the new text (see [Notes](../guide/notes.md#export-import-and-deleting)).

## Characters with a meaning

The backslash, the backtick and `* _ # + - . ! [ ] ( ) < > |` can mean something. To show one as it is, put a backslash before it: `\*not italic\*`, `1\. not a list`. In code (backticks) no backslash is needed.

## What the preview does not show

The text stays as written; only the preview differs from GitHub:

- **HTML** (`<b>`, `<kbd>`, `<details>` …) is not supported. Something that looks like a tag, `List<Item>` outside backticks, can even hide the rest of the paragraph.
- **Footnotes** (`[^1]`), **emoji** codes (`:smile:`) and **highlighting** (`==text==`) stay plain text.
- **Images** (`![name](https://…)`) from the web are not loaded.
- `_text_` is underlined, not italic (see [Text](#text)).

## An example

```markdown
## Gold
- Class `PlayerInventory`, field `gold` (int)
- `PlayerInventory:AddGold (int)` – script *Gold +1000*
- Pointer: `game.exe+0x4040 → 0x28 → 0x0`

## Character
| Value | Offset | Type   |
| ----- | -----: | ------ |
| HP    |  `0x4` | int32  |
| Mana  | `0x14` | float  |

## Open
- [x] Gold found
- [ ] What resets the stamina? Trace *Sprint*, see `StaminaComponent`
```

The [notes page](../guide/notes.md) shows how this looks in the preview.
